name: Ethical and Professional Standards
blurb: The CFA Institute Code of Ethics and the seven Standards of Professional Conduct (2024 edition), tested as short scenarios where you must spot the exact rule, the exact remedy and the exact timing.
accaNote: ACCA gave you the IESBA principles (integrity, objectivity, competence and due care, confidentiality, professional behaviour) and a threats-and-safeguards mindset. The CFA Standards are more specific and investment-focused (insider information, trade allocation, personal trading, soft dollars, use of the CFA marks), so nothing here is fast-tracked.

modules.title: Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession
modules.summary: Why the investment business runs on trust, what makes it a profession, why well-meaning people still cross ethical lines, and the four-step framework for making ethical decisions.

acca.note: BT and SBL covered ethics, professional values and stakeholder thinking. New for CFA: the trust-and-profession framing, the named challenges to ethical behaviour (overconfidence, situational influences, short-term focus) and the Identify–Consider–Act–Reflect framework.

lessons.title: Ethics, trust and what makes a profession

cards.title: What ethics means here
cards.body:
**Ethics** is a set of moral principles that guide behaviour. It asks what is *right*, not only what is *allowed*. Ethical conduct weighs your own interests against the effect on other people.

A **code of ethics** writes down a group's principles so that members, clients and the public know what to expect. **Standards of conduct** set the minimum behaviour required, and they are enforced.

Exam angle: a code states values and sets a floor. It can't list every situation, so you still have to use judgement.

cards.title: Why trust is the product
cards.body:
Clients can't easily see what an adviser does with their money or judge how good the advice is. This is **information asymmetry**, so clients hand over assets largely on trust.

When trust is high, more people invest, markets are deeper and capital is cheaper. When scandals erode it, investors pull out or demand higher returns, and everyone in the industry pays.

One professional's misconduct therefore imposes costs on the whole profession. That is why CFA Institute polices conduct.

cards.title: What makes an occupation a profession
cards.body:
Typical features:
- specialised knowledge and skills built through education and experience
- admission standards (exams, required experience)
- a code of ethics and standards of conduct
- monitoring and enforcement of members' conduct (self-regulation)
- a commitment to serve clients and society, not only yourself
- ongoing development of the body of knowledge

Investment management is a younger profession than medicine or law. In many places you can practise without holding a professional credential.

cards.title: Legal vs ethical
rows: Often require more than the law
Lag behind new products and practices
Principles apply to new situations straight away
Some ethical acts may break a rule or contract (e.g., whistleblowing)

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body:
ACCA (through IESBA) taught you five fundamental principles: integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, and professional behaviour. You applied them through a threats-and-safeguards framework.

The CFA Code has six components and seven Standards. The Standards are enforceable and are tested as scenarios. Expect investment-specific duties that ACCA never examined: inside information, trade allocation, priority of personal trades, soft dollars and use of the CFA marks.

lessons.title: Why good people slip, and a framework for deciding

cards.title: Challenges to ethical behaviour
cards.body:
Most violations are committed by ordinary people, not villains. Three common traps:
- **Overconfidence**: “I'm an ethical person, so what I'm doing must be fine.” People overrate their own ethics and stop questioning their choices.
- **Situational influences**: money (bonuses), prestige, loyalty to a boss or team, peer pressure, fear of losing your job. They are strongest when you don't notice them.
- **Short-term focus**: chasing this quarter's numbers and ignoring long-term consequences.

Noticing these pressures is the first line of defence.

cards.title: Rules alone are not enough
cards.body:
A firm that relies only on a detailed rulebook teaches staff to ask “Is it legal? Is it allowed?” Rules can't anticipate every new product or situation, so people stop thinking once nothing forbids an action.

A strong **ethical culture** adds a tone from the top, incentives aligned with clients' interests, and permission to raise concerns. Your decisions affect clients, your employer, colleagues, the market and the profession, so think about all of them.

cards.title: The ethical decision-making framework
cards.body:
Four steps:
- **Identify**: the facts, the stakeholders and the duties owed to each, the relevant ethical principles, and any conflicts of interest.
- **Consider**: situational influences, extra guidance (compliance, colleagues, the Code and Standards), and alternative actions.
- **Act**: decide, then carry out the action or escalate.
- **Reflect**: did the outcome match what you expected? What would you do differently?

The steps repeat: reflection feeds into your next decision.

cards.title: The framework applied
cards.body:
Ana, a junior analyst, is told by her boss to raise a rating to Buy because the bank is pitching for the issuer's bond deal.
- **Identify**: she owes clients objective research. Banking revenue conflicts with research independence.
- **Consider**: pressure from her boss and fear for her career. She can ask compliance. Her options include keeping the rating, documenting her reasoning, or escalating.
- **Act**: she keeps the rating her analysis supports and raises the issue with compliance.
- **Reflect**: did escalation work? Does the firm need a firewall?

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: LM1 questions are conceptual. They test the order of the framework steps, which factors count as situational influences, and why ethical ≠ legal. Remember the order as **I-CAR**: Identify → Consider → Act → Reflect. Seeking guidance and weighing alternatives belong to **Consider**, not Identify.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between laws and ethical standards?
options: Conduct that complies with the law is, by definition, ethical.
Ethical standards apply only where no law exists.
Ethical standards often require more than the law requires.
questions.explanation: Laws set a minimum level of acceptable behaviour. Ethical standards often go further. Legal conduct is not automatically ethical, because laws lag new practices and some legal acts still harm clients. Ethics also applies where laws exist, not only in gaps.

questions.stem: Why does misconduct by a few investment professionals tend to harm the industry as a whole?
options: Regulators automatically fine every firm in the industry after a scandal.
It reduces investors' trust, so they participate less and demand higher returns, which raises costs for everyone.
It harms only the clients directly involved, so the effect on the industry is minimal.
questions.explanation: The investment business depends on trust because of information asymmetry. When trust falls, investors withdraw or demand a higher return, which raises the cost of capital and cuts the industry's business. There is no automatic industry-wide fine, and the damage spreads beyond the clients directly involved.

questions.stem: Which feature most distinguishes a profession from an ordinary occupation?
options: Members commit to a code of ethics whose standards are monitored and enforced.
Members earn above-average compensation.
Members work only for regulated firms.
questions.explanation: A profession is marked by specialised knowledge, admission standards and an enforced code of conduct that puts clients and society first. High pay and working at regulated firms do not by themselves make an occupation a profession.

questions.stem: An adviser says: “Everything I recommend is legal, so I have met my ethical obligations.” This view is best described as:
options: correct, because laws define ethical conduct in financial markets.
incomplete, because legal conduct can still fall short of ethical standards.
correct, as long as the adviser also follows firm policy.
questions.explanation: Legality is the minimum. A legal but unsuitable, high-fee or misleading recommendation can still be unethical. Firm policies are also only rules, and they can't anticipate every situation, so following them does not complete the ethical analysis.

questions.stem: In the ethical decision-making framework, considering alternative actions and seeking additional guidance belong to which step?
options: Identify
Reflect
Consider
questions.explanation: The steps are Identify (facts, stakeholders, duties, conflicts), Consider (situational influences, guidance, alternatives), Act, and Reflect (review the outcome and the lessons). Seeking guidance and weighing alternatives belong to Consider.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager whose bonus depends on quarterly peer rankings is tempted to buy a speculative stock just before quarter-end to lift reported performance. Which challenge to ethical behaviour does this best illustrate?
options: A situational influence combined with a short-term focus
A conflict between local law and the Code and Standards
Overconfidence in the manager's investment skill
questions.explanation: The bonus is a situational influence (money), and the quarter-end deadline creates short-term focus. No legal conflict is described. Overconfidence in ethics means believing you're too ethical to slip. Here the pressure comes from incentives, not self-belief.

questions.stem: Which statement about overconfidence as a challenge to ethical behaviour is most accurate?
options: People tend to overrate their own ethics, which makes them less likely to question their own decisions.
Overconfidence affects only inexperienced professionals.
Overconfidence is a situational influence created by compensation schemes.
questions.explanation: Overconfidence is an internal bias: we assume our own conduct is ethical and stop checking it. It affects experienced people as much as new ones, sometimes more. Compensation schemes are external situational influences, not overconfidence.

questions.stem: A firm relies only on a detailed rulebook and makes no effort to build an ethical culture. Its employees are most likely to:
options: need no personal judgement, because the rules cover every case.
ask only whether an action is allowed, and miss situations the rules don't cover.
commit fewer violations than employees at firms with a principles-based culture.
questions.explanation: Rules can't anticipate every situation. A purely rule-based culture encourages “Is it legal or allowed?” thinking, which leaves gaps for new products and grey areas. Judgement is still needed, and there is no reason to expect fewer violations.

questions.stem: A firm pays its sales staff larger bonuses for selling its in-house funds, which charge higher fees than comparable external funds. Under the ethical decision-making framework, what should a salesperson do first?
options: Act by recommending the in-house funds, because they are legal products.
Reflect on past sales to judge whether clients were satisfied.
Identify the conflict between the incentive and the duties owed to clients.
questions.explanation: The framework starts with Identify: the facts, the stakeholders, the duties owed to them and any conflicts. Here the bonus conflicts with the duty to put clients first. Acting before analysing skips steps. Reflect comes last and looks back at a decision already made.

questions.stem: Which is least likely to be a benefit of high ethical standards in the investment profession?
options: Greater willingness of investors to take part in markets
A lower cost of capital for issuers
Guaranteed higher investment returns for clients
questions.explanation: Trust encourages participation, deepens markets and lowers the return investors demand, so capital becomes cheaper. Ethics cannot guarantee investment returns, and claiming it can would itself be a misrepresentation.

questions.stem: Laws differ across countries and are slow to cover new financial products. This is the strongest argument that:
options: a principles-based code of ethics is needed to guide conduct where the law is silent or unclear.
professionals should follow the most lenient applicable law so they stay competitive.
codes of ethics are needed only in countries without securities laws.
questions.explanation: Because laws vary and lag innovation, principles are needed to guide behaviour in gaps and new situations. Following the most lenient law reverses the Code's stricter-rule principle. Codes matter in every jurisdiction, not only where there is no law.

questions.stem: A manager says: “I've been in this business 20 years. I know where the lines are, so I don't need to run this trade past compliance.” This most likely illustrates:
options: peer pressure
overconfidence
short-term focus
questions.explanation: Believing your experience makes you immune to ethical error, and so skipping checks, is overconfidence. No colleagues are pushing him, so this isn't peer pressure, and nothing in the statement is about short-term results.

questions.stem: In the Reflect step of the ethical decision-making framework, a professional should most likely:
options: establish the relevant facts and the stakeholders affected.
seek guidance from compliance before choosing a course of action.
assess whether the outcome matched expectations and what can be learned for future decisions.
questions.explanation: Reflect comes after Act and looks back at the result to improve future decisions. Establishing facts and stakeholders is Identify. Seeking guidance before deciding is Consider.

flashcards.front: Four steps of the ethical decision-making framework
flashcards.back: Identify → Consider → Act → Reflect (“I-CAR”).
Overconfidence (in your own ethics), situational influences (money, prestige, loyalty, peer pressure), short-term focus.
Laws set the minimum. Ethical standards often require more. Legal ≠ ethical, and laws lag new products and differ by country.
Information asymmetry means clients rely on trust. Higher trust → more participation and a lower cost of capital. Misconduct by a few hurts the whole profession.
Specialised knowledge, admission standards, a code of ethics, monitoring and enforcement, service to clients and society, ongoing development of knowledge.

modules.title: Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct
modules.summary: Who must follow the CFA Institute Code and Standards, the six components of the Code, the map of the seven Standards (2024 edition), and how the Professional Conduct Program enforces them.

acca.note: ACCA has its own code and disciplinary process, but the CFA Code's six components, the seven Standards, the 2024 changes and the Professional Conduct Program are all new.

lessons.title: The Code (6 components) and the Standards (7 groups)

cards.title: Who is bound
cards.body:
All CFA Institute **members**, including charterholders, and all **CFA Program candidates** must follow the Code and Standards. Non-members are not bound, but a member who helps a non-member break the rules is.

The **Code of Ethics** sets out six broad principles. The **Standards of Professional Conduct** are seven groups of specific, enforceable rules, with 23 sub-standards since 2024. The *Standards of Practice Handbook* explains how they apply.

cards.title: The Code of Ethics: six components
cards.body:
Members and candidates must:
- act with integrity, competence, diligence and respect, and ethically, toward everyone in the markets
- put the integrity of the profession and clients' interests above their own
- use reasonable care and independent professional judgement
- practise, and encourage others to practise, in a professional and ethical manner
- promote the integrity and viability of global capital markets
- maintain and improve their own competence, and help others do the same

cards.title: The seven Standards
rows: A Knowledge of the Law · B Independence and Objectivity · C Misrepresentation · D Misconduct · E Competence
A Material Nonpublic Information · B Market Manipulation
A Loyalty, Prudence, and Care · B Fair Dealing · C Suitability · D Performance Presentation · E Preservation of Confidentiality
A Loyalty · B Additional Compensation Arrangements · C Responsibilities of Supervisors
V Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions
A Diligence and Reasonable Basis · B Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients · C Record Retention
A Avoid or Disclose Conflicts · B Priority of Transactions · C Referral Fees
VII Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate
A Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs · B Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program

cards.title: What changed on 1 January 2024
cards.body:
- **New I(E) Competence**: act with, and maintain, the competence your responsibilities require.
- **V(B) expanded**: you must now disclose the **nature of the services** you provide and their **costs** to the client.
- **VI(A) renamed Avoid or Disclose Conflicts**: avoid conflicts where reasonably possible. Otherwise disclose them fully and fairly, prominently, and in plain language.

Older study material shows 22 sub-standards and “Disclosure of Conflicts”. Don't learn from it.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: The Code states aspirational principles. The Standards are the specific rules you are tested on. Most questions describe a scenario and ask whether there is a violation, or which Standard applies, so know the map well. The 2027 curriculum gives each Standard group its own learning module.

cards.title: How CFA Institute enforces the Standards
cards.body:
The **Professional Conduct Program (PCP)** investigates possible violations under the CFA Institute Bylaws and Rules of Procedure. Professional Conduct staff do the investigating. The **Disciplinary Review Committee (DRC)**, a committee of volunteer members, oversees the process and supplies hearing panels.

Two principles guide every case: a **fair process** for the member or candidate, and **confidentiality** of the proceedings.

cards.title: What triggers an investigation
cards.body:
- Self-disclosure on the annual **Professional Conduct Statement (PCS)**, e.g., a customer complaint, regulatory action, lawsuit or criminal charge
- Written complaints from clients, employers, colleagues or others
- Evidence of misconduct in the media or other public sources
- Reports from exam proctors
- CFA Institute's own analysis of exam materials and monitoring of websites and social media

Poor investment performance on its own is not misconduct.

cards.title: Outcomes and sanctions
cards.body:
After investigating (which may include requests for documents or interviews), staff may:
- close the case with no disciplinary action
- issue a **cautionary letter**
- continue investigating
- propose a **disciplinary sanction**

If a sanction is proposed, the member or candidate can accept it or reject it. A rejected sanction goes to a **hearing panel**, which decides. Sanctions include public censure, suspension of membership and of the right to use the designation, and revocation of the charter. Candidates can be suspended or barred from the program.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Cooperating with the PCP, including sharing confidential client information it needs, does **not** breach III(E) Confidentiality. Members are **encouraged**, not required, to report other people's violations to CFA Institute, unless the law requires reporting.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: The process looks like ACCA's: a complaint, then an investigation, then a disciplinary panel. The differences: CFA members **certify their conduct every year** on the PCS, and **candidates** can be disciplined too, for example for exam misconduct, before they ever earn the charter.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a component of the Code of Ethics rather than a specific Standard?
options: Maintain and improve professional competence and strive to improve the competence of others.
Disclose referral fees to clients before entering any formal agreement for services.
Keep records supporting investment recommendations for at least seven years.
questions.explanation: Maintaining and improving competence is the sixth component of the Code. Disclosing referral fees is Standard VI(C). Seven-year retention is a recommended procedure under V(C), not part of the Code.

questions.stem: Which change took effect with the 2024 revision of the Code and Standards?
options: The Priority of Transactions standard was removed.
A stand-alone Competence standard was added under Professionalism.
GIPS compliance became mandatory under Performance Presentation.
questions.explanation: The 2024 revision added I(E) Competence, added disclosure of services and costs to V(B), and renamed VI(A) “Avoid or Disclose Conflicts”. VI(B) Priority of Transactions still exists. GIPS compliance remains recommended, not required, under III(D).

questions.stem: Who is required to comply with the CFA Institute Code and Standards?
options: Only CFA charterholders
All employees of firms that employ at least one charterholder
CFA Institute members and CFA Program candidates
questions.explanation: The Code and Standards bind all members, including charterholders, and all candidates. Candidates are covered before they earn the charter. Colleagues who are not members or candidates are not bound, although a member may not help them break the rules.

questions.stem: Under the 2024 wording of Standard VI(A), how should a member deal with a conflict of interest?
options: Avoid it where reasonably possible. Otherwise make full and fair disclosure that is prominent and in plain language.
Disclose it. Avoidance is never required.
Always avoid it. Disclosure is no longer an acceptable remedy.
questions.explanation: The renamed “Avoid or Disclose Conflicts” makes avoidance the preferred route where reasonably possible. Disclosure remains acceptable when avoidance isn't, but it must be prominent, in plain language and effective. Each distractor takes only one half of the rule.

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely to trigger a Professional Conduct Program investigation?
options: A member discloses on her Professional Conduct Statement that a client has sued her over investment advice.
A member's portfolio underperforms its benchmark for two years.
A newspaper reports that a member misled investors about a fund's fees.
questions.explanation: Investigations start from self-disclosure on the PCS, written complaints, public reports of misconduct, proctor reports and CFA Institute's own monitoring. Underperformance on its own is not misconduct. The lawsuit and the press report both point to possible violations.

questions.stem: Professional Conduct staff conclude that a member violated the Standards and propose a sanction. The member rejects it. What happens next?
options: The matter is referred to a hearing panel, which decides the case.
The sanction takes effect automatically after 30 days.
The case is closed, because a sanction requires the member's agreement.
questions.explanation: If a member or candidate rejects a proposed sanction, a hearing panel drawn from the Disciplinary Review Committee reviews the case and decides. Rejection does not make the sanction automatic, and it does not end the case.

questions.stem: Which outcome of a Professional Conduct inquiry does not involve a disciplinary sanction?
options: Public censure
Revocation of the charter
A cautionary letter
questions.explanation: Staff can close a case with no action, issue a cautionary letter, continue investigating, or propose a sanction. A cautionary letter is not a disciplinary sanction. Public censure and revocation are sanctions.

questions.stem: Which two principles guide the Professional Conduct Program?
options: Speed, and public transparency of all inquiries
Fairness to the member or candidate, and confidentiality of the proceedings
Deterrence, and maximum publicity of alleged violations
questions.explanation: The process is built on fair treatment of the person under investigation and on confidentiality. Inquiries are not made public while they are under way. Only certain final sanctions, such as public censure, are published.

questions.stem: Which Code of Ethics component most directly requires a member to put clients' interests ahead of personal interests?
options: Use reasonable care and exercise independent professional judgement.
Place the integrity of the investment profession and the interests of clients above their own personal interests.
Promote the integrity and viability of the global capital markets.
questions.explanation: The second component explicitly ranks the profession's integrity and clients' interests above personal interests. Reasonable care and independent judgement concern how analysis is done. Promoting market integrity concerns the markets as a whole.

questions.stem: A newly registered Level I candidate argues that she is not yet subject to the Standards because she is not a charterholder. She is:
options: wrong, because candidates must comply with the Code and Standards.
right, until she passes Level I.
right, except for Standard VII(A) on exam conduct.
questions.explanation: The Code and Standards apply to all members and candidates. A candidate is bound from the moment she enrols, and every Standard applies to her, not just VII(A).

questions.stem: Which statement about the Professional Conduct Statement (PCS) is most accurate?
options: Only candidates file it, when they register for an exam.
Members file it only when they change employer.
Members file it every year and disclose matters such as complaints and legal or regulatory proceedings related to their professional conduct.
questions.explanation: Members must file the PCS annually, disclosing complaints, litigation, regulatory or criminal matters and confirming they follow the Code and Standards. Filing it is also a condition of keeping the right to use the designation. Candidates make a similar statement at registration, so the PCS is not limited to candidates or to job changes.

questions.stem: A charterholder's client agreement describes the services she provides but says nothing about her fees. Which Standard most directly addresses this omission?
options: V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts
questions.explanation: Since 2024, V(B) requires members to disclose the nature of their services and the costs to the client. Fees are not in themselves a conflict of interest under VI(A). III(A) is the broad duty of loyalty, but V(B) is the specific rule on disclosing costs.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Code and the Standards is most accurate?
options: The Standards apply only to charterholders, and the Code applies only to candidates.
The Code states broad principles. The Standards set out specific conduct that members and candidates must follow.
Where local law and the Standards differ, local law always overrides the Standards.
questions.explanation: The Code is a set of principles, and the Standards are enforceable rules. Both apply to all members and candidates. Under I(A), when law and Standards conflict, the stricter one applies, so local law does not always win.

flashcards.back: Integrity, competence and respect · clients and the profession first · reasonable care and independent judgement · practise and encourage ethical conduct · promote market integrity · maintain and improve competence.

modules.title: Guidance for Standard I: Professionalism
modules.summary: I(A) follow the stricter of law and Code and dissociate from violations; I(B) keep independence and objectivity (gifts, issuer-paid research, pressure); I(C) don't misrepresent; I(D) no professional dishonesty; I(E) act with the competence your role needs.

acca.note: IESBA integrity, objectivity, competence and due care (AA, SBL) map loosely onto I(B), I(C) and I(E). New for CFA: the stricter-rule test, dissociation instead of external reporting, the source-of-gift distinction, the conditions for issuer-paid research and the scope of I(D).

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
Understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules and regulations, including the Code and Standards, of any government, regulator, licensing body or professional association that governs your professional activities.

- If the law and the Code and Standards **conflict**, follow the **stricter** one.
- Don't **knowingly participate or assist** in any violation.
- **Dissociate** from any violation you become aware of.

cards.title: The stricter rule wins
cards.body:
Priya, CFA, works in a country whose law lets advisers omit personal holdings when recommending a stock. The Standards are stricter, so she must avoid or disclose the conflict under VI(A).

Her colleague works where the law demands disclosure of **all** holdings in covered companies, however small. The law is stricter there, so he follows it.

If a country has **no** securities law, apply the Code and Standards.

cards.title: Dissociation
cards.body:
If you learn that colleagues or clients are breaking the law or the Standards:
- raise it with your supervisor or compliance
- refuse to take part, and remove your name from affected reports
- in extreme cases, **resign**

Staying silent while you keep working on the matter is **not** dissociation. Reporting to regulators or CFA Institute is **encouraged but not required** unless the law requires it. Being *asked* to do something wrong is not a violation. Doing it is.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: You don't have to be a lawyer or know every law in every country. You need to know the laws that govern your own activities, and you should ask compliance or legal counsel when unsure. “My boss told me to” is no defence: knowingly assisting an employer's illegal act violates I(A).

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: ACCA's NOCLAR rules (responding to non-compliance with laws and regulations) can require escalation and sometimes disclosure to an authority. CFA I(A) requires **dissociation**. Reporting outside the firm is encouraged but generally not required, unless local law requires it.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
Use reasonable care and judgement to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity. Don't offer, solicit or accept any gift, benefit, compensation or consideration that could reasonably be expected to compromise **your own or someone else's** independence and objectivity.

The test: would a reasonable person think it could sway your judgement? Modest gifts and ordinary business entertainment are fine.

cards.title: Gifts: who gives matters
rows: Client, thanking you for past service
May accept. Disclose to your employer, ideally beforehand.
Client, offering a bonus for future results
Needs your employer's written consent first: IV(B)
Issuer, broker or fund seeking your business

cards.title: Issuer-paid research and travel
cards.body:
Being paid by a company to write research on it is allowed if:
- you receive a **flat fee** agreed in advance, not linked to your conclusion or rating
- the issuer-paid arrangement is **disclosed** in the report

On company visits, pay your own travel and use **commercial transport**. Accept issuer-arranged transport, such as a corporate jet, only when no commercial option exists. Avoid lavish hospitality.

cards.title: Pressure points
cards.body:
- **Sell side**: investment banking wants favourable ratings for its clients. Use firewalls and separate reporting lines. If the firm can't publish an objective view, it can put the issuer on a **restricted list** and stop publishing on it, rather than publish only positive views. Analysts' pay should not depend on banking deals.
- **Buy side**: pressure to rate stocks the fund already holds favourably, and choosing external managers because of gifts.
- Credit raters and performance measurers must likewise resist pressure from the parties they assess.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: IESBA treats gifts and hospitality through threats and safeguards, accepting only those that are “trivial and inconsequential”. CFA's test is whether a gift could “reasonably be expected to compromise” independence. CFA also cares a lot about the **source**: a client's thank-you gift is acceptable with disclosure to the employer, while a similar gift from an issuer is not.

lessons.title: I(C) Misrepresentation, I(D) Misconduct, I(E) Competence

cards.title: I(C) Misrepresentation
cards.body:
Don't **knowingly** misrepresent your investment analysis, recommendations, actions or other professional activities. This covers anything written, spoken, emailed or posted on social media, as well as **omissions** that make a statement misleading.

It includes overstating your qualifications or your firm's services, and **guaranteeing** returns on investments that are uncertain. Stating a guarantee is fine only when the instrument really carries one, such as a principal-protected structured product, and you describe it accurately.

cards.title: Plagiarism
cards.body:
Using someone else's research, models, charts or words without credit is misrepresentation, even if you reword them. You may use others' work if you **cite** the author and source.

Work you did for a former employer belongs to that employer, so you can't present it as your own. If you use third-party research, you still need a reasonable basis for relying on it under V(A).

cards.title: I(D) Misconduct
cards.body:
Don't engage in professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud or deceit, or any act that reflects adversely on your **professional** reputation, integrity or competence.

Violations: padding expense claims, lying to clients, repeatedly coming to work intoxicated, a conviction for fraud.

Usually not violations: an arrest for peaceful civil disobedience, or personal bankruptcy with no fraud or deceit involved. Personal behaviour is outside I(D) unless it bears on your professional integrity.

cards.title: I(E) Competence (new in 2024)
cards.body:
Act with, and maintain, the competence your professional responsibilities require. Competence means **knowledge, skills and abilities**, judged against the **role** you are actually doing.
- A poor investment outcome is **not** proof of incompetence.
- Degrees alone don't make you competent. Taking on work you aren't equipped for, such as a GIPS verification or a review of ESG managers, is a violation.
- No specific continuing-education hours are required. Keep up as your role changes, get expert help, or decline the work.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: I(C) needs a **knowing** misrepresentation. An honest error that you correct promptly is not a violation. I(D) is about professional dishonesty, so don't apply it to every personal-life choice. Under I(E), losing money is not the test. Accepting work beyond your competence is.

questions.stem: Laila, CFA, lives in Country X, which has no securities laws. She manages money for clients in Country Y, whose securities law is less strict than the Code and Standards. Which rules should she follow?
options: Country Y's law
Country X's law
The Code and Standards
questions.explanation: Under I(A), she follows the stricter of the applicable law and the Code and Standards. Country X has no law, and Country Y's law is less strict, so the Code and Standards are the strictest applicable rules.

questions.stem: Mara, CFA, finds that her firm is executing trades that breach several clients' written investment mandates. She tells her supervisor, who dismisses the issue. Mara then keeps working on the accounts and does nothing more. Has she complied with the Standards?
options: Yes. Telling her supervisor fully discharged her duty.
Yes. She is not personally responsible for the firm's trading decisions.
No. After her supervisor fails to act, she must dissociate further, for example by going to compliance and refusing to take part.
questions.explanation: Dissociation means taking real steps to separate yourself from a violation: escalating to compliance, refusing to take part and, in extreme cases, resigning. Raising it once and then carrying on with the affected work is not enough. Because she knowingly keeps working on the accounts, she can't rely on not being responsible for the firm's decisions.

questions.stem: Ben, CFA, recommends a stock to clients while owning shares of it. His local regulations allow advisers to leave personal holdings out of their recommendations. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Ben must avoid or disclose the conflict, because the Standards are stricter than local law.
Ben need not disclose anything, because local law governs.
Ben must sell the shares, because the 2024 Standards no longer allow disclosure.
questions.explanation: Under I(A), the stricter rule applies. VI(A) requires him to avoid the conflict or fully disclose it, which is stricter than local law. Selling is one way to avoid the conflict, but it isn't mandatory. Prominent, plain-language disclosure is still acceptable under the 2024 wording.

questions.stem: Do the Standards require a member to report a colleague's securities-law violation to the regulator?
options: Yes, within 30 days of discovering the violation.
No. Reporting is encouraged and may be required by local law, but the Standards themselves don't require it.
Yes, but only to CFA Institute, not to the regulator.
questions.explanation: I(A) requires dissociation, not external reporting. Reporting to regulators or CFA Institute is encouraged, and the law may require it in some places. There is no 30-day rule and no mandatory report to CFA Institute.

questions.stem: After Sofia, CFA, publishes a Buy rating on a company, its investor-relations team sends her two championship-final tickets worth $3,000. Would accepting them most likely violate the Standards?
options: Yes, it would violate I(B).
No, as long as she discloses the gift to her employer.
No, because she issued the rating before the gift arrived.
questions.explanation: A gift of this value from a company she covers could reasonably be expected to compromise her objectivity in future reports, and disclosure doesn't cure it. Disclosure to the employer is the remedy for gifts from clients, not from issuers. The rating coming first doesn't matter, because she will keep covering the company.

questions.stem: A client gives his portfolio manager a weekend at a resort to thank him for strong returns last year. The manager tells his employer before accepting. Has he violated the Standards?
options: Yes. Accepting any gift above nominal value from a client violates I(B).
Yes. He needed his employer's written consent under IV(B).
No. A client's gift for past service is acceptable when disclosed to the employer.
questions.explanation: Gifts from clients for past performance pose little threat to independence, so I(B) allows them with disclosure to the employer. IV(B) written consent is needed when compensation depends on **future** performance or competes with the employer, which isn't the case here.

questions.stem: An issuer hires Wen, CFA, to write a research report on it. She receives a flat fee plus a bonus if the share price rises within three months of publication. Is this acceptable?
options: Yes, provided she discloses the arrangement in the report.
No. The bonus links her pay to the effect of her research.
Yes, because issuer-paid research is permitted.
questions.explanation: Issuer-paid research is permitted only for a flat fee that doesn't depend on the conclusion or its effect. A bonus tied to the share price rewards a favourable report and compromises her objectivity. Disclosure doesn't fix a pay structure that is itself compromising.

questions.stem: The head of investment banking at Dev's broker-dealer asks to see Dev's draft report on a banking client and suggests he raise the rating because a bond deal is pending. Dev, CFA, should most appropriately:
options: raise the rating, but disclose the banking relationship in the report.
share the draft and accept the suggestion, because banking revenue is also in his employer's interest.
keep the rating his analysis supports. If the firm can't publish an objective view, it should put the company on a restricted list.
questions.explanation: I(B) requires research to stay independent of banking pressure. Disclosing the relationship doesn't make a pressured rating objective. The firm can restrict publication instead of issuing biased research. Serving the employer never justifies compromising objectivity.

questions.stem: A fund company's brochure says: “Our corporate bond fund guarantees 6% a year.” The fund holds corporate bonds of varying credit quality. This is most likely:
options: a violation of I(C), because the returns of a bond portfolio are not guaranteed.
not a violation, if the fund has earned at least 6% every year for the past decade.
not a violation, because bonds pay fixed coupons.
questions.explanation: Fixed coupons don't guarantee the return of a credit-risky portfolio, because of defaults, price changes and reinvestment risk. Calling an uncertain return guaranteed is misrepresentation, and a good track record doesn't change that.

questions.stem: A charterholder declares personal bankruptcy after the restaurant he owned on the side fails. There was no fraud or deceit. Has he violated I(D) Misconduct?
options: Yes. Bankruptcy reflects adversely on his competence as an adviser.
No. Personal bankruptcy without dishonesty doesn't on its own reflect on his professional integrity.
Yes, unless he discloses the bankruptcy to his clients.
questions.explanation: I(D) covers professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud or deceit, or conduct that reflects on professional integrity. A business failure without deceit is not misconduct. A bankruptcy involving fraud would be.

questions.stem: Lena holds a PhD in physics and runs an equity portfolio. She accepts a paid engagement to perform a GIPS verification for another firm, although she has no knowledge of the GIPS standards. She has most likely violated:
options: nothing, because her advanced degree shows her competence
I(C) Misrepresentation, but only if her verification report contains errors
I(E) Competence
questions.explanation: I(E) requires the knowledge, skills and abilities the specific role demands. A degree in another field doesn't qualify her to verify GIPS compliance. Accepting the work is the violation, whether or not errors later appear.

questions.stem: Ravi copies several paragraphs of analysis from an independent research firm's industry report into his own report. He changes some wording and gives no citation. Has he violated the Standards?
options: No. The report was available to the public.
Yes. Rewording doesn't remove the need to credit the source, so this is plagiarism under I(C).
No, as long as he checked the data independently.
questions.explanation: Presenting another person's analysis as your own is misrepresentation, even if the source is public and the wording is changed. Checking the data helps under V(A) but doesn't make the analysis his. He must cite the author.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager follows her fund's stated process carefully, but the fund trails its benchmark by 8% over the year. Has she violated I(E)?
options: No. A poor outcome alone doesn't show a lack of competence.
Yes. Underperformance this large shows a lack of competence.
Yes, unless she completes extra continuing-education hours.
questions.explanation: The guidance is explicit: competent professionals can still suffer losses. I(E) looks at whether she had and used the competence her role needs, not at the result. The Standard doesn't prescribe any specific number of CE hours.

questions.stem: Omar, CFA, lives in Country A, whose securities law is stricter than the Code and Standards. He does business in Country B, whose law is less strict than the Code. Country A's law says that the law of the place where business is conducted governs. Which rules must Omar follow in Country B?
options: Country A's law
Country B's law
The Code and Standards
questions.explanation: Country A's law points to Country B's law. Country B's law is less strict than the Code, so the stricter rules are the Code and Standards. Country A's law doesn't apply to this business on its own terms, and Country B's law is too weak.

questions.stem: A broker that executes many of a portfolio manager's trades invites him on a five-day golf trip at a luxury resort. The manager pays his own airfare, and the broker pays for the resort and golf. Has the manager violated the Standards?
options: Yes. Accepting the lavish resort stay could reasonably be expected to compromise his objectivity in choosing brokers.
No. He paid for his own air travel.
No. I(B) applies only to sell-side analysts.
questions.explanation: Lavish hospitality from a party that wants his business threatens his independence, here his choice of brokers. Paying for the flights doesn't offset the value of five days at a luxury resort. I(B) applies to buy-side professionals too.

questions.stem: Kai's firm website still lists tax planning and estate planning among its services, although the specialist who provided them left and the firm stopped offering them. Kai, CFA, knows this but doesn't ask for the page to be updated. Has he violated the Standards?
options: No. Website content is the marketing department's responsibility.
Yes. Knowingly letting the firm misstate its services violates I(C).
No, as long as clients who ask for tax planning are told it's no longer available.
questions.explanation: I(C) covers knowingly misrepresenting services, including by leaving out of date information in place. Kai knows the listing is false, so blaming another department doesn't excuse him. Telling clients only when they ask still leaves prospects misled by the page.

questions.stem: A charterholder regularly drinks heavily at lunch and is visibly impaired in afternoon client meetings. Which statement is most accurate?
options: She is violating I(D) Misconduct.
She isn't violating the Standards, because alcohol use is a personal matter.
She is violating I(C) Misrepresentation.
questions.explanation: Behaviour that impairs her professional work and reflects on her competence falls under I(D). Personal conduct becomes a Standards issue when it affects professional duties. Nothing she has said is misleading, so I(C) doesn't fit.

questions.stem: An issuer pays Jae, CFA, a disclosed flat fee, agreed in advance, to write research on it. The issuer also offers its corporate jet to fly her to a remote mine. Commercial flights to the site run twice a week. Jae accepts the jet. Has she violated the Standards?
options: No, because her fee was flat and disclosed.
No, because the trip was for genuine research.
Yes, because commercial transport was available.
questions.explanation: The fee arrangement is compliant. The travel is a separate issue: under I(B), analysts should use commercial transport where it exists and accept issuer-provided travel only when no alternative is available. A genuine research purpose doesn't cure the conflict.

questions.stem: Nia, CFA, learns that her supervisor is backdating client trade tickets. Which action best meets her obligations under the Standards?
options: Report it straight to the regulator, as the Standards require.
Report it to compliance and refuse to take part, and resign if the problem continues.
Do nothing unless she personally processes the backdated tickets.
questions.explanation: I(A) requires her to dissociate from a known violation: escalate internally, refuse to take part and, in the extreme, leave. The Standards encourage but don't require reporting to regulators. Doing nothing because she isn't directly involved isn't dissociation.

flashcards.back: Follow the stricter of the applicable law and the Code and Standards. Where there is no securities law, follow the Code and Standards.
Escalate to your supervisor or compliance → refuse to take part and remove your name → resign in extreme cases. Reporting to regulators is encouraged, not required (unless the law requires it).
Flat fee agreed in advance, not linked to the conclusion or price outcome, and disclosed in the report.
Gift for past service: may accept, disclose to employer (I(B)). Bonus for future performance: needs the employer's written consent (IV(B)).
Pay your own way and use commercial transport. Issuer-provided transport only if no commercial option exists. No lavish hospitality.
Knowing misrepresentation in any form, including omissions, guarantees of uncertain returns, overstated qualifications and plagiarism (rewording without credit still counts).
Professional dishonesty, fraud or deceit, or acts reflecting on professional integrity. Personal bankruptcy without fraud, or peaceful civil disobedience, usually isn't a violation.
Act with and maintain the knowledge, skills and abilities your role needs. A bad outcome ≠ incompetence. No mandated CE hours. Decline work beyond your competence.

modules.title: Guidance for Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets
modules.summary: II(A) don't trade on, or tip, material nonpublic information (mosaic theory is allowed); II(B) don't distort prices or volume with intent to mislead.

acca.note: ACCA LW touches on insider dealing as a criminal offence, but the CFA tests (material and nonpublic, the mosaic theory, firewalls, and intent to mislead in manipulation) are new.

lessons.title: II(A) Material Nonpublic Information and the mosaic theory

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
If you hold information that is **material** and **nonpublic** and could affect an investment's value, you must not **act** on it or **cause others to act** on it. That means no trading and no tipping.

It doesn't matter how you got the information: from an insider, a client, a friend or an overheard conversation. The rule also covers related instruments, such as options, bonds and other companies whose value depends on the news.

cards.title: Is it material? Is it nonpublic?
rows: Would it likely move the price, or would a reasonable investor want to know it? Is it specific, and is the source reliable?
Unannounced earnings, M&A, regulatory approvals, dividend changes, a major contract won or lost
Has it been released to the market in general?
Told only to a few analysts or investors; heard privately from a CFO; overheard at dinner

cards.title: Mosaic theory
cards.body:
You **may** act on a conclusion you reach by combining **public** information with **non-material nonpublic** information, even if that conclusion would be material if the company announced it.

Example: your channel checks, store visits, supplier conversations and public data all suggest sales are slowing, so you downgrade. That's good research, not insider trading. Keep records showing how you reached the view (V(C)), because they prove the mosaic.

cards.title: Firm safeguards
cards.body:
- **Firewalls** (information barriers) between corporate finance and research or trading
- **Watch lists** (trades monitored) and **restricted lists** (no trading or recommendations)
- Pre-clearance and review of personal and proprietary trades
- Limiting who has access to deal information

If a firm has no firewall, it should restrict trading in the issuer. If you receive MNPI, encourage the company to make it public, and don't trade until it is.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Telling only a group of analysts is still **nonpublic**. An influential analyst's unpublished rating change can itself be MNPI. An **expert network** consultant who works at the issuer's supplier may pass on MNPI, so ask about industry trends, not company secrets.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: ACCA LW covered insider dealing as a criminal offence. CFA II(A) is broader and more precise: the information must be **both** material and nonpublic, the mosaic theory is expressly allowed, and the duty is not to **act or cause others to act**. Keeping the information confidential isn't enough on its own.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
Don't engage in practices that **distort prices** or **artificially inflate trading volume** with the **intent to mislead** market participants. There are two types:
- **Information-based**: spreading false or misleading information, such as rumours, fake reports, or pump-and-dump (hype a stock you hold, then sell into the rise).
- **Transaction-based**: trades that give a false impression of price or volume, such as wash trades, marking the close, or cornering supply to squeeze other traders.

cards.title: Intent is the key
cards.body:
Legitimate strategies that move prices are fine: arbitrage, large block trades to rebalance, tax-loss selling, hedging and genuine liquidity provision. The question is whether the trader **intended to mislead** others about price, volume or supply.

Example violation: trading a thinly traded bond back and forth between two accounts you manage so that it looks actively traded. A good motive, such as “helping liquidity”, doesn't excuse a false impression.

cards.title: Spot the manipulation
cards.body:
- A manager buys heavily in the last minutes of the quarter to push up the closing prices of fund holdings → **marking the close** (violation).
- An analyst buys call options, then posts that a company “is about to be taken over”, which is untrue → **information-based** manipulation (violation).
- A fund sells a losing stock in December to realise a tax loss and buys a similar, not identical, stock → **legitimate** (no intent to mislead).

cards.title: Squeezes and corners
cards.body:
Building a dominant position in a security, or in the deliverable supply behind a derivative, in order to force short sellers or counterparties to pay artificially high prices is manipulation, even though every trade is real.

A large position isn't the problem in itself. The violation is using it to control the price.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: If the stem gives a genuine economic reason for a trade (rebalancing, tax, hedging, client orders), there is no II(B) violation. If the purpose is to create apparent activity or a price that doesn't reflect real supply and demand, it is a violation, whatever the motive. An honest forecast that turns out wrong is not manipulation.

questions.stem: At a restaurant, Ines, CFA, overhears two executives discussing an unannounced takeover bid for TargetCo at a 40% premium. She buys TargetCo shares for her clients. Has she violated the Standards?
options: No. She didn't receive the information in confidence from an insider.
No. The trades were for clients, not for her own account.
Yes, she has violated II(A). The information is material and nonpublic, however she obtained it.
questions.explanation: II(A) covers any material nonpublic information, however it was obtained, including by chance. A takeover premium is clearly material, and the bid hasn't been announced. Acting for clients is still acting on MNPI.

questions.stem: An analyst counts trucks at a company's plant, reviews its public filings and talks with retail customers. She concludes that earnings will miss consensus and changes her rating to Sell. Has she violated II(A)?
options: No. The mosaic theory allows conclusions drawn from public and non-material nonpublic information.
Yes. Her conclusion is material and hasn't been made public.
Yes, unless she first shares her conclusion with the company.
questions.explanation: Each piece of her information is public or immaterial on its own. Combining them into a material conclusion is exactly what the mosaic theory permits. She doesn't need the company's approval to publish her view.

questions.stem: In a one-on-one meeting, a CFO tells an analyst that next quarter's sales will come in 15% below consensus. The company hasn't announced this. What should the analyst do?
options: Send the information to all clients at once so that every client is treated fairly.
Not trade or recommend based on it, and encourage the company to disclose it publicly.
Trade on it only for client accounts, because II(A) is about personal gain.
questions.explanation: This is MNPI, given selectively. The analyst must not act or cause others to act, and should urge public disclosure. Sending it to clients would cause others to act on it, and II(A) has no exception for trades made for clients.

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely to be material nonpublic information?
options: An analyst's conclusion about margin pressure, drawn from public industry data and her own store visits
An unannounced drug approval known to a company insider
A dividend cut revealed only to a small group of institutional investors
questions.explanation: The analyst's own conclusion built from public and immaterial information is a legitimate mosaic. The drug approval is material and unannounced. Selective disclosure to a few investors doesn't make the dividend cut public.

questions.stem: A fund manager holds a thinly traded stock. To make it more liquid, he trades shares back and forth at market prices between two funds he manages, raising the reported volume. Has he violated the Standards?
options: No. The trades were made at market prices.
No. His aim was to help investors, not harm them.
Yes. The trades artificially inflate volume and mislead market participants.
questions.explanation: Trades with no real change in ownership, made to create apparent volume, are transaction-based manipulation. Market prices don't make them genuine, and II(B) has no exception for good intentions when the activity is designed to give a false impression.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of information-based market manipulation?
options: Buying a large block of shares to rebalance an index fund
Posting false takeover rumours to lift a stock's price, then selling
Selling shares at year-end to realise a tax loss
questions.explanation: Spreading false information to move a price is information-based manipulation (pump-and-dump). Index rebalancing and tax-loss selling are legitimate trades with an economic purpose, not attempts to mislead.

questions.stem: Near expiry, a trader buys up 80% of the deliverable supply of the commodity underlying a futures contract. She then demands delivery from short holders, and the price spikes. Has she violated the Standards?
options: Yes. She used a dominant position to squeeze the shorts.
No. Every purchase was a genuine trade.
No. Commodity markets are outside the Standards.
questions.explanation: Cornering supply to force counterparties to pay artificially high prices is transaction-based manipulation, even though each trade is real. II(B) covers all markets, including commodities and derivatives.

questions.stem: An analyst publishes an honest but mistaken report forecasting strong earnings. The stock rises, then falls when earnings disappoint. Has the analyst violated II(B)?
options: Yes. The report distorted the price.
No. There was no intent to mislead.
Yes. The forecast proved wrong.
questions.explanation: II(B) needs intent to mislead. An honest forecast that turns out wrong is not manipulation. The analyst may need to review the diligence behind it under V(A), but that is a separate question.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager pays an expert-network consultant who works at a supplier to TechCo. The consultant reveals that TechCo has just cancelled a large order, which TechCo hasn't announced. The manager sells TechCo. Has he violated the Standards?
options: No. The information came from the supplier, not from TechCo.
No. He paid for the information through a legitimate expert network.
Yes, he has violated II(A).
questions.explanation: The cancelled order is material to TechCo and hasn't been made public. The source doesn't matter: MNPI from a supplier, customer or consultant is still MNPI. Paying through an expert network doesn't make it public.

questions.stem: A CEO gives new earnings guidance during a webcast that was announced in advance and is open to anyone. An analyst listening trades on the guidance during the webcast. Has the analyst violated II(A)?
options: Yes. She must wait 24 hours after any announcement before trading.
No. Information released through a widely accessible channel is public.
Yes. Only analysts were likely to be listening.
questions.explanation: Information becomes public once it is released to the market in general. A pre-announced webcast open to all investors does this. The Standards set no fixed waiting period, and the open access makes this different from selective disclosure.

questions.stem: A well-known analyst at a large firm plans to downgrade a stock, and her ratings regularly move prices. Before the report is published, she tells a colleague on the trading desk, who sells the firm's proprietary position. Has a violation occurred?
options: Yes. Her unpublished downgrade is material nonpublic information.
No. The information came from the firm's own research.
No. Proprietary trades are for the employer, not for clients.
questions.explanation: A rating change that is likely to move the price is material, and before publication it is nonpublic. Tipping the trading desk causes others to act on it, which violates II(A). Trading the firm's account before clients receive the report also puts the employer ahead of clients, contrary to III(A) and III(B).

questions.stem: Which procedure is most effective at preventing misuse of material nonpublic information between a firm's M&A advisory team and its research department?
options: Requiring employees to promise not to discuss deals
Letting research see deal information as long as reports disclose the relationship
Information barriers that restrict physical and electronic access, plus watch and restricted lists monitored by compliance
questions.explanation: Firewalls with access controls, backed by watch and restricted lists, are the main recommended procedures under II(A). Promises without controls are weak. Disclosure doesn't permit acting on MNPI.

questions.stem: On the last trading day of the quarter, a fund manager buys large volumes of a stock the fund already holds, aiming to lift its closing price and the fund's reported performance. Which statement is most accurate?
options: He has not violated the Standards, because the trades were at prevailing market prices.
He has violated II(B) Market Manipulation.
He has violated II(A) Material Nonpublic Information.
questions.explanation: This is marking the close: trading to distort a price, here to flatter reported performance. Executing at market prices doesn't make it legitimate. No inside information is involved, so II(A) doesn't apply.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions most likely violates the Standards?
options: Publishing a well-researched Buy recommendation on a stock the analyst owns, with the ownership clearly disclosed
Buying a large position gradually over several days to limit the effect on the price
Posting under a pseudonym that “insiders say a buyout is imminent”, with no such information, and selling after the price jumps
questions.explanation: The pseudonymous rumour is false information spread to move the price: information-based manipulation under II(B). The disclosed, well-researched recommendation is compliant. Spreading a large order over time is a legitimate way to reduce market impact.

flashcards.back: When its release would likely move the price, or a reasonable investor would want it. Consider how specific it is and how reliable the source is.
Until it has been released to the market in general. Selective disclosure to a few analysts or investors is still nonpublic.
Acting on a conclusion drawn from public plus non-material nonpublic information is permitted, even if the conclusion is material. Keep records.

flashcards.front: What to do if you receive MNPI
flashcards.back: Don't trade and don't tip. Encourage the issuer to release it publicly, and tell compliance.
Firewalls (information barriers), watch lists, restricted lists, pre-clearance and monitoring of personal and proprietary trades.
Information-based (false rumours, pump-and-dump) and transaction-based (wash trades, marking the close, cornering or squeezes).
Intent to mislead. Legitimate trades (tax, rebalancing, hedging, arbitrage) are fine even if they move prices.

modules.title: Guidance for Standard III: Duties to Clients
modules.summary: III(A) loyalty, prudence and care (who the client is, soft dollars, proxies); III(B) fair dealing in dissemination and trade allocation; III(C) suitability and the IPS; III(D) fair, accurate and complete performance; III(E) confidentiality and its three exceptions.

acca.note: IESBA confidentiality and due care give a little head start. Fiduciary ordering, soft dollars, proxy voting, trade allocation, IPS-based suitability and performance-presentation rules are new.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
Clients are owed **loyalty**, **reasonable care** and **prudent judgement**. Act for their benefit and put their interests **before your employer's and your own**. The order is clients → employer → you.

Know what your role requires: an adviser with discretion owes more than someone who only executes orders. Follow any applicable fiduciary law, but the Standards may be stricter.

cards.title: Who is the client?
cards.body:
- **Pension plan**: the duty is owed to the plan's **participants and beneficiaries**, not to the sponsoring company or its management.
- **Fund or mandate**: manage to the stated mandate for the fund's investors.
- **Trust**: the beneficiaries.

Classic exam trap: a pension manager who votes proxies or picks investments to please the sponsor's CEO.

cards.title: Soft dollars and brokerage
cards.body:
Commissions are paid out of client assets, so brokerage is the **client's asset**.
- Use soft dollars only for **research that benefits the client**, not for office rent, travel or marketing.
- Seek **best execution**.
- If a client **directs** brokerage to a particular broker, follow the instruction but disclose that best execution may not be achieved.
- Using client commissions to pay for referrals of new clients benefits the firm, not the client, and violates III(A).

cards.title: Proxy voting and other duties
cards.body:
Voting proxies is part of the duty of loyalty. Vote in clients' interests under a written policy that is disclosed to them. A **cost–benefit analysis** may justify not voting some proxies, for example where voting abroad blocks the shares from trading.

Also: don't churn accounts to generate fees, don't put the firm's interests ahead of clients', and follow each client's mandate and constraints.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: ACCA's objectivity and due care map loosely onto this. CFA III(A) is a **fiduciary-style ranking**: client before employer before self. Expect scenarios on soft dollars, directed brokerage, proxy voting and pension beneficiaries, none of which ACCA examined.

lessons.title: III(B) Fair Dealing and III(C) Suitability

cards.title: III(B) Fair Dealing
cards.body:
Deal **fairly and objectively** with all clients when sharing analysis, making recommendations and taking investment action.

Fair doesn't mean equal. You may offer **premium service levels**, such as more contact or deeper research, if the tiers are **disclosed** and available to every client willing to pay, and other clients aren't disadvantaged. No client may get a trading head start on a new or changed recommendation.

cards.title: Dissemination and allocation
cards.body:
- **Recommendations**: send new or changed recommendations to all relevant clients **at the same time**. Keep the gap between decision and release short. Don't phone favoured clients first.
- **Block trades**: allocate **pro rata** to order size, at the same average price.
- **Hot IPOs**: allocate pro rata to all clients for whom the issue is suitable. Don't keep shares for yourself, your family or favoured clients if other clients then get less.
- Have written allocation policies and record order times.

cards.title: III(C) Suitability
cards.body:
In an advisory relationship:
- (a) **before** acting, make reasonable inquiry into the client's experience, return and risk objectives and constraints, and reassess regularly
- (b) make sure each investment fits the client's written objectives and constraints (usually an **IPS**)
- (c) judge suitability in the context of the **whole portfolio**

When managing to a **mandate or style**, act only within the stated strategy. The fund manager doesn't assess the suitability of each investor in the fund.

cards.title: Unsolicited trades
cards.body:
If a client asks for an unsuitable trade, explain why it's unsuitable.
- If the effect on the total portfolio is **small**, you may carry it out after the explanation and document the discussion.
- If it is **large**, discuss updating the IPS. You may get the client's written acknowledgement, or decline and follow firm policy.

Don't silently go along with it, and don't silently refuse.

cards.title: Style drift
cards.body: A fund marketed as “large-cap value” starts buying small-cap tech stocks because they are rising. Even if returns improve, the manager has violated III(C): investors chose the fund for its mandate. Changing strategy requires disclosure and notice to investors in advance, and V(B) also applies.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: III(B) is about treating **clients** fairly relative to each other. VI(B) is about clients relative to **you**. A member who puts IPO shares in her own account usually breaches both. A member who favours large clients over small ones breaches III(B).

lessons.title: III(D) Performance Presentation and III(E) Confidentiality

cards.title: III(D) Performance Presentation
cards.body:
Make reasonable efforts to ensure performance information is **fair, accurate and complete**. Don't:
- cherry-pick the best accounts or periods
- present simulated, back-tested or model results as actual
- drop terminated accounts to improve the numbers
- claim a previous firm's record as your new firm's without disclosure
- show gross returns without saying they are gross

This applies to anyone presenting performance, in a pitch meeting or on social media too.

cards.title: Best practice vs requirement
cards.body:
Complying with the **GIPS** standards is the recommended way to meet III(D), but III(D) does **not** require it.

In a brief presentation, such as a one-page ad or a post, you may show limited data if you state that **full details are available on request**. Disclose whether returns are gross or net of fees, the benchmark used, and any use of leverage or model results.

cards.title: III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
cards.body:
Keep information about **current, former and prospective** clients confidential unless:
- the information concerns **illegal activities** by the client
- **disclosure is required by law**, such as a court order or a regulator's demand
- the client **permits** disclosure

Sharing information with CFA Institute's **Professional Conduct Program** during an investigation is **not** a breach.

cards.title: Confidentiality in practice
cards.body: The duty continues after the relationship ends. Keep client data secure. Don't discuss clients in public or on social media: even an anecdote with the name removed can identify a client. If you're unsure whether the law requires disclosure, ask compliance or legal counsel. If you learn of a client's illegal activity, I(A) may also require you to dissociate.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: IESBA confidentiality is similar: disclosure is allowed with client authorisation, when the law requires it, or under a professional duty or right. CFA explicitly adds a client's **illegal activity** as an exception, confirms that cooperating with the **PCP** is fine, and extends the duty to **prospective** clients.

questions.stem: A pension plan's investment manager votes the plan's shares against a proposal that would benefit plan participants, because the sponsoring company's CEO asked him to. Has he violated the Standards?
options: Yes, he has violated III(A). His duty runs to plan participants and beneficiaries, not to the sponsor.
No. The sponsor hires the manager, so the sponsor is the client.
No. Proxy voting is outside the Standards.
questions.explanation: For a pension plan, loyalty is owed to the participants and beneficiaries. Proxy voting is part of the fiduciary duty and must serve their interests. Voting to please the sponsor's management breaches III(A).

questions.stem: A manager uses soft dollars to pay for a research database used in managing client portfolios, and for an upgrade to the firm's office lease. Which statement is correct?
options: The database is permitted. The office lease is not.
Both are permitted if they are disclosed to clients.
Neither is permitted, because soft dollars may pay only for trade execution.
questions.explanation: Client brokerage may pay for research that benefits clients. Office rent is a firm overhead that benefits the manager, not clients, and disclosure doesn't make it acceptable. Soft dollars aren't limited to execution: client-benefiting research is explicitly allowed.

questions.stem: A client tells her manager to send all of her trades to her brother-in-law's brokerage, which charges above-market commissions. The manager should:
options: refuse, because the instruction conflicts with best execution.
follow the instruction without comment, because client brokerage belongs to the client.
follow the instruction and disclose to the client that best execution may not be achieved.
questions.explanation: Directed brokerage is allowed because the brokerage is the client's asset. The manager must still tell her it may cost more or reduce execution quality. Refusing ignores her right to direct her own asset. Saying nothing leaves out the required disclosure.

questions.stem: A manager routes client trades to a broker that charges above-market commissions because the broker refers new clients to the manager's firm. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation if the commissions are within the industry range.
This violates III(A), because it uses client brokerage to benefit the firm.
This isn't a violation, because new clients help existing clients through economies of scale.
questions.explanation: Brokerage belongs to clients and must be used for their benefit (best execution, research). Paying more to win referrals for the firm puts the firm first. Indirect benefits to existing clients don't justify it.

questions.stem: An analyst changes her rating on a stock from Buy to Sell. She phones her five largest clients first, then emails all other clients an hour later. Has she violated the Standards?
options: No. Premium clients can get earlier service if they pay higher fees.
No. An hour is a reasonable gap between them.
Yes, she has violated III(B) Fair Dealing.
questions.explanation: Recommendation changes must reach all clients at the same time, or in a way that doesn't disadvantage anyone. An hour's head start lets the large clients trade first. Premium tiers can buy more service, but not the chance to trade ahead of other clients.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager receives fewer shares of an oversubscribed IPO than she ordered. She gives all of them to her largest accounts. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This violates III(B). She should allocate pro rata among all suitable accounts that ordered.
This isn't a violation if the largest accounts pay the highest fees.
This isn't a violation if all clients are told about the allocation afterwards.
questions.explanation: Partly filled orders, especially for hot IPOs, should be allocated pro rata among the accounts for which the issue is suitable. Fee size doesn't justify favouritism. Telling clients afterwards doesn't make an unfair allocation fair.

questions.stem: A firm offers a “platinum” service with monthly calls and detailed reports for a higher fee. The offer is disclosed and available to all clients. Does this violate III(B)?
options: Yes. All clients must receive identical service.
No. Different service levels are allowed when disclosed and available to all clients.
No, but only because platinum clients are institutional investors.
questions.explanation: Fair dealing doesn't mean equal treatment. Premium tiers are acceptable when disclosed and open to every client willing to pay, provided other clients aren't disadvantaged, for example by getting recommendations later. The type of client is irrelevant.

questions.stem: A retired client with a conservative, low-risk IPS calls and asks his adviser to put 2% of his portfolio into a speculative biotech stock. What should the adviser do?
options: Explain that the stock is unsuitable. Because the effect on the overall portfolio is small, she may then carry out the trade and document the discussion.
Refuse, because the trade is inconsistent with the IPS.
Carry out the trade and update the IPS to an aggressive risk profile.
questions.explanation: For an unsolicited trade that is small relative to the portfolio, the adviser explains why it's unsuitable and may then execute it. Refusing outright isn't required. Changing the IPS because of one small trade would misstate the client's real objectives.

questions.stem: The manager of an emerging-market equity index fund puts 15% of the fund into US technology stocks to boost returns. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation if the fund beats its index.
This isn't a violation, because suitability applies only to individual advisory clients.
This violates III(C), because the holdings are inconsistent with the fund's mandate.
questions.explanation: III(C)(2) requires managers who run money to a stated mandate to stay within it. Holding stocks outside the index is style drift, whatever the result. Suitability covers mandated portfolios as well as advisory relationships.

questions.stem: A manager's marketing material shows the returns of her three best accounts as “representative” and leaves out seven accounts in the same strategy that underperformed. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation if the three accounts' returns are accurate.
This violates III(D).
This isn't a violation, because the firm doesn't claim GIPS compliance.
questions.explanation: Cherry-picking accounts makes the presentation unfair and incomplete, even if each number is accurate. III(D) applies whether or not the firm claims GIPS compliance.

questions.stem: At a conference, a member shows a one-page summary of composite returns and says full performance details are available on request. Does this violate III(D)?
options: Yes. III(D) requires a full GIPS-compliant presentation at all times.
Yes. Brief presentations of performance are prohibited.
No. A brief presentation is acceptable when full information is offered.
