questions.explanation: Limited presentations are allowed if they are fair and accurate and the member makes the full information available. GIPS compliance is recommended, not required. Short presentations are not banned.

questions.stem: An adviser's former client, whose account closed two years ago, is being sued. A journalist asks about the client's portfolio, and the adviser shares the details because “he's no longer a client.” Which statement is most accurate?
options: This violates III(E). The duty of confidentiality covers former clients.
This isn't a violation, because the relationship has ended.
This isn't a violation, because the lawsuit is public.
questions.explanation: Confidentiality covers current, former and prospective clients and continues after the relationship ends. A public lawsuit doesn't make the account details public, and a journalist's request is not a legal requirement to disclose.

questions.stem: During a Professional Conduct investigation into a member's conduct, CFA Institute asks for relevant client account records. The member:
options: must refuse unless each client consents in writing.
may provide them. Cooperating with the PCP doesn't breach III(E).
may provide them only if a court orders it.
questions.explanation: The Standards expressly allow sharing confidential information with the Professional Conduct Program, which keeps it confidential. Client consent and court orders are separate routes, and neither is needed here.

questions.stem: A manager handles her father's account, which pays the firm's standard fees. When allocating shares of a hot IPO, she leaves her father's account out to avoid any appearance of favouritism, although the issue suits it. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation. VI(B) requires family accounts to be excluded.
This isn't a violation, because leaving out a family member can never disadvantage a client.
This violates III(B). Fee-paying family accounts should be treated like any other client account.
questions.explanation: A fee-paying family account is a client account and must be treated like any other: neither favoured nor disadvantaged. VI(B) limits accounts where the member has a beneficial interest getting priority. It doesn't require penalising a regular client who happens to be a relative.

questions.stem: A client recently retired and inherited a large sum. Her manager hasn't updated her IPS in three years and keeps managing to the old objectives. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation, because the client didn't ask for an update.
This violates III(C). Suitability must be reassessed regularly and after material changes.
This isn't a violation, because IPS reviews are only a recommended practice.
questions.explanation: III(C)(1)(a) requires the adviser to reassess and update the client's circumstances regularly. Retirement and a large inheritance are material changes that call for a review. The adviser can't wait for the client to ask.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager leaves her firm and starts a new one. Her marketing presents the returns of the strategy she ran at her old firm as the new firm's composite record, with no disclosure that they were earned elsewhere. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This violates III(D).
This isn't a violation, because she made all the investment decisions.
This isn't a violation if the new firm claims GIPS compliance.
questions.explanation: Presenting another firm's results as your own firm's record, without disclosure, misleads prospects about whose performance it is. Even if she made the decisions, the record belongs to the old firm unless the history is properly disclosed and supported. Claiming GIPS compliance wouldn't change this.

questions.stem: Under a written policy disclosed to clients, a manager doesn't vote proxies for small foreign holdings where voting would block the shares from trading for several weeks. Has the manager violated the Standards?
options: Yes. Every proxy must be voted.
No. A cost–benefit analysis can justify not voting some proxies.
Yes, unless each client votes the shares himself.
questions.explanation: Proxy voting is part of loyalty, but managers may skip votes whose cost, such as losing the ability to trade, outweighs the benefit, provided the policy is disclosed. There is no rule that every proxy must be voted.

questions.stem: A manager suspects a client is laundering money through his account. Local law requires reporting suspicious transactions, and she files a report without telling the client. Has she violated the Standards?
options: No. Disclosure is permitted because it is required by law and concerns illegal activity.
Yes. She breached III(E), because the client didn't give permission.
Yes. She breached III(A), because loyalty to the client rules out reporting.
questions.explanation: III(E) allows disclosure when the information concerns a client's illegal activities or when the law requires it, and both apply here. Loyalty never requires helping a client break the law.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager runs a high-yield bond fund that is managed to its stated mandate. A retiree puts 60% of her savings into the fund. Has the manager violated III(C)?
options: Yes. He must assess the suitability of each investor in the fund.
Yes. He must change the fund's strategy, because high-yield bonds are unsuitable for retirees.
No. His duty is to manage the fund in line with its mandate, not to assess each investor's suitability.
questions.explanation: When managing to a mandate, the manager's suitability duty is to stay within the fund's stated objectives and constraints. Advisers who recommend the fund to individuals have their own suitability duties. Changing the strategy would breach the mandate.

flashcards.back: Clients → employer → self.

flashcards.front: III(A): who is the client of a pension manager?
flashcards.back: The plan participants and beneficiaries, not the sponsoring company or its management.

Brokerage is the client's asset. Use it only for research that benefits clients, with best execution. Directed brokerage: follow the client's instruction, and disclose that best execution may not be achieved.
Fair ≠ equal. Premium service tiers are OK if disclosed and available to all. Recommendations go to all clients at the same time. Allocate block trades and IPOs pro rata.
Explain that it's unsuitable. If small relative to the portfolio, you may execute and document. If large, discuss updating the IPS, get written acknowledgement, or decline per firm policy.
Act only in line with the stated strategy (no style drift). You don't assess each fund investor's suitability.
No. It is recommended. III(D) requires fair, accurate and complete performance information. Brief presentations are OK if full details are offered on request.
Client illegal activity · disclosure required by law · client permission. Cooperating with the PCP is not a breach. Covers current, former and prospective clients.

modules.title: Guidance for Standard IV: Duties to Employers
modules.summary: IV(A) loyalty to your employer (independent practice, leaving to compete, whistleblowing); IV(B) written consent for outside compensation; IV(C) supervisors must make reasonable efforts to prevent and detect violations.

acca.note: ACCA LW covers employee duties of fidelity and restrictive covenants in general terms. The CFA rules on what you may and may not do before leaving, written consent for outside pay and supervisor duties are new.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
In matters related to your employment, act for your **employer's benefit**. Don't deprive the employer of your skills and abilities, reveal confidential information, or otherwise cause harm.

Loyalty to an employer never requires breaking the law or harming clients or the market: **clients come first**. Nor does it require giving up important personal or family obligations.

cards.title: Independent practice
cards.body:
Before you start providing services for pay that compete with your employer, such as managing money for friends for a fee or consulting at weekends, **notify** your employer. Describe the services, how long they'll last and the pay. Then get the employer's **consent** before you start.

Unpaid volunteer work that doesn't compete with the employer isn't an issue.

cards.title: Leaving an employer
rows: Plan; interview; register a new firm; lease an office
Soliciting current clients or prospects; taking client lists, files, models or records; setting up the new business on the employer's time
Contacting former clients using public information or your memory (unless a non-compete applies); using your general skills and experience
Using records or confidential information taken from the employer; breaching a valid non-compete or non-solicit agreement

cards.title: Whistleblowing, contractors, social media
cards.body:
Revealing your employer's illegal or unethical conduct to protect clients or market integrity is **not** a loyalty breach. Leaking information for personal gain is.

Independent contractors owe the same loyalty to the firms that hire them.

Professional social-media accounts and contacts built for the employer usually belong to the firm. Follow firm policy when you leave.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Planning to leave is not a violation. Soliciting clients **before** you leave is. Taking records is a violation even if you created them, such as your own spreadsheets or client contact list, because they are employer property (V(C) as well). Remembering clients' names after you leave and finding them through public directories is fine if there is no non-compete.

lessons.title: IV(B) Additional Compensation and IV(C) Supervisors

cards.title: IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements
cards.body:
Don't accept gifts, benefits, compensation or consideration that **competes with** your employer's interest, or might reasonably be expected to **create a conflict** with it, **unless you get written consent from all parties involved**.

Get the consent **before** accepting, after disclosing the nature, amount and duration of the arrangement. Email counts as written. Typical cases: a client's bonus for beating a benchmark, a paid board seat, outside consulting.

cards.title: I(B) vs IV(B) vs VI(C)
rows: A gift could compromise your objectivity
Decline it if it could sway you. Disclose client gifts to your employer.
Outside pay could conflict with your employer's interest
Get written consent from your employer (all parties) first
Disclose to employer, clients and prospects before the engagement

cards.title: IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors
cards.body:
Anyone with supervisory authority must make **reasonable efforts** to ensure that the people they supervise comply with laws, rules, regulations and the Code and Standards. That includes supervisees who aren't CFA members.

Reasonable efforts mean adequate compliance procedures that are implemented and enforced, plus training and monitoring. You can delegate tasks, but not your responsibility.

cards.title: When something goes wrong
cards.body:
If you learn of a possible violation, **investigate promptly**. Limit the person's activities and increase supervision while you investigate. Don't simply rely on the employee's promise that it won't happen again.

If the firm's compliance system is **inadequate**, decline supervisory responsibility **in writing** until adequate procedures are adopted.

A subordinate's violation is not automatically the supervisor's. The supervisor violates IV(C) only if reasonable efforts weren't made.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: IV(B) consent must be **written** and must come **before** acceptance. Verbal approval or telling the employer afterwards fails. IV(C) applies to anyone who supervises, not only compliance officers, and it includes overseeing outside service providers the supervisor is responsible for.

questions.stem: Before resigning, a portfolio manager leases office space and registers a new advisory firm. He doesn't contact any clients until after he resigns. Has he violated IV(A)?
options: Yes. Registering a competing firm while employed is disloyal.
Yes, unless he told his employer about each step.
No. Preparing to compete is allowed.
questions.explanation: Members may prepare to leave and compete, for example by registering a firm or leasing space, as long as they don't solicit clients, take employer property or neglect their duties while still employed. Telling the employer about each preparatory step isn't required.

questions.stem: Two weeks before leaving her firm, an analyst emails her top clients that she is leaving and invites them to move their accounts to her new firm. Has she violated the Standards?
options: No, as long as she doesn't take any client files.
Yes, she has violated IV(A) by soliciting clients while still employed.
No. Clients are free to choose their manager.
questions.explanation: Soliciting current clients before leaving deprives the employer of business while she is still being paid to serve it. That violates IV(A) even if she takes no records. Clients' freedom to move doesn't permit her to solicit them while she is still employed.

questions.stem: On her last day, a portfolio manager copies a client contact spreadsheet she built herself onto a USB drive. Has she violated the Standards?
options: Yes. The records belong to her employer.
No. She created the spreadsheet herself.
No, if she deletes it after contacting the clients.
questions.explanation: Records created in the course of employment are employer property, whoever made them. Taking them violates IV(A), and V(C) too. Deleting the file later doesn't undo the misappropriation.

questions.stem: An employee manages money for friends at weekends for a share of the profits and doesn't tell his employer, an investment management firm. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation, because the work is done in his own time.
This isn't a violation, as long as the friends aren't the firm's clients.
This violates IV(A). He must notify his employer and get consent before paid independent practice that competes with it.
questions.explanation: Managing money for pay competes with his employer's business, whatever the hours or whoever the clients. IV(A) requires notice describing the services, duration and pay, and the employer's consent before he starts.

questions.stem: A client offers his portfolio manager a $20,000 bonus if the portfolio beats its benchmark this year. The manager tells his supervisor verbally, the supervisor agrees, and he accepts. Has he complied with the Standards?
options: Yes. His supervisor approved the arrangement.
No. Written consent is required.
Yes. The bonus is aligned with the client's interest, so there is no conflict.
questions.explanation: A client bonus for future performance could create a conflict with the employer's interest, for example by encouraging him to favour that client. IV(B) requires written consent from all parties before he accepts. Verbal approval isn't enough.

questions.stem: An analyst is invited to join the board of a local company for an annual fee. Before accepting, she gets written consent from her employer. Has she complied with IV(B)?
options: Yes, she has complied with IV(B).
No. Members may not serve on corporate boards.
No, unless all of her clients also consent in writing.
questions.explanation: IV(B) is met by getting written consent from the employer before accepting outside paid work. Members may serve on boards. Client consent isn't required, although she may need to disclose the board seat to clients under VI(A) if it could affect her work for them.

questions.stem: A supervisor learns that a trader she oversees front-ran client orders. The trader promises not to do it again, and the supervisor takes no further action. Has the supervisor violated the Standards?
options: No. The trader has corrected his behaviour.
Yes, she has violated IV(C).
No. Responsibility lies with the compliance department.
questions.explanation: Once a supervisor knows of a violation, she must investigate promptly and take steps such as limiting the trader's activities and increasing monitoring. Relying on his promise isn't a reasonable effort. Supervisors can't hand this responsibility to compliance.

questions.stem: A newly appointed head of research finds that the firm has no written compliance procedures. What is the best action?
options: Accept the role and rely on each analyst's professional judgement.
Accept the role, and report the firm to CFA Institute.
Decline supervisory responsibility in writing until adequate procedures are adopted.
questions.explanation: Under IV(C), a supervisor can't make reasonable efforts without an adequate compliance system. She should decline the responsibility in writing and press the firm to adopt procedures. Relying on individual judgement isn't supervision. Reporting to CFA Institute isn't required and doesn't fix the gap.

questions.stem: Standard IV(C) applies to:
options: any member or candidate with supervisory authority, including authority over employees who aren't members.
only compliance officers.
only the supervision of other CFA members and candidates.
questions.explanation: IV(C) applies to anyone who supervises others, and it covers everyone they supervise, whether or not those people are bound by the Standards. Compliance officers are covered only if they have supervisory authority.

questions.stem: After leaving her firm, a portfolio manager with no non-compete agreement contacts former clients, finding them through a public directory and her memory. Has she violated the Standards?
options: Yes. She must wait one year before contacting former clients.
No, she has not violated the Standards.
Yes. Former clients' identities are her ex-employer's confidential information.
questions.explanation: Without a non-compete or non-solicit agreement, a former employee may contact former clients using public sources and her own memory. She must not use records taken from the employer. The Standards set no waiting period.

questions.stem: An analyst discovers that her employer is misrepresenting performance to clients. Internal escalation fails, and she reports the matter to the regulator, providing supporting documents. Has she violated the Standards?
options: Yes, she has violated IV(A) by revealing confidential employer information.
Yes, she has violated III(E) by passing on client data.
No. Protecting clients and market integrity takes precedence over loyalty to the employer.
questions.explanation: Whistleblowing to protect clients or the integrity of the market is consistent with the Standards. Loyalty to an employer doesn't extend to covering up misconduct. Disclosing information to a regulator about illegal activity falls within the confidentiality exceptions.

questions.stem: A client offers her portfolio manager free use of her vacation home for one week a year whenever the portfolio's annual return exceeds 10%. What should the manager do?
options: Get written consent from his employer before accepting.
Tell his employer about the arrangement at the end of the year.
Decline, because all gifts from clients are prohibited.
questions.explanation: A benefit that depends on future performance is additional compensation that could conflict with the employer's interest, for example by encouraging him to favour this client. IV(B) requires written consent before he accepts. Telling the employer later is too late. Client gifts aren't banned outright.

questions.stem: The head of trading delegates monitoring of personal trading to a junior compliance analyst and never reviews the results. A trader then breaks the personal trading rules. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Delegation moved the responsibility to the junior analyst.
The head of trading has no responsibility, because compliance is a separate function.
The head of trading remains responsible. Tasks can be delegated, but supervisory responsibility cannot.
questions.explanation: Under IV(C), supervisors may delegate tasks but stay responsible for making reasonable efforts to prevent and detect violations. Never reviewing the delegated work is not a reasonable effort.

questions.stem: A firm hires an independent contractor to build a valuation model. The contract states that the firm owns the model. After the project, the contractor sells the model to a competitor. Has the contractor violated the Standards?
options: Yes, the contractor has violated IV(A).
No. Contractors aren't employees.
No. The contractor built the model with her own skills.
questions.explanation: IV(A) covers independent contractors, who owe loyalty to the firms that hire them. Under the contract the model belongs to the firm, so selling it to a competitor misappropriates the firm's property, whatever skills went into building it.

questions.stem: An analyst takes approved family leave during a critical project. Her manager says she has violated her duty of loyalty. Is the manager right?
options: Yes. She deprived her employer of her skills and abilities.
No. IV(A) doesn't require putting the employer ahead of important personal and family obligations.
Yes, unless she works remotely during the leave.
questions.explanation: The guidance makes clear that loyalty to an employer doesn't require giving up important personal or family obligations. Taking approved leave isn't depriving the employer of her skills in the IV(A) sense.

flashcards.back: Allowed: plan, register a firm, lease an office. Not allowed while employed: soliciting clients or prospects, taking any records (even ones you made). After leaving: contact former clients from memory or public sources unless a non-compete applies.
Notify the employer (services, duration, pay) and get consent before starting paid work that competes with the employer.
Disclosing employer wrongdoing to protect clients or the market is consistent with the Standards. Doing it for personal gain is not.
Written consent from all parties (in practice, the employer) before accepting compensation or benefits that compete or conflict with the employer's interest. Disclose nature, amount and duration.
Decline supervisory responsibility in writing until adequate procedures exist.
Investigate promptly, limit the person's activities, increase supervision. Don't rely on the employee's promise. Tasks can be delegated, responsibility can't.

modules.title: Guidance for Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions
modules.summary: V(A) be diligent and have a reasonable basis (third-party research, group reports, models, outside managers); V(B) communicate services, costs, process, risks and fact vs opinion; V(C) keep supporting records.

acca.note: IESBA due care and the audit idea of sufficient appropriate evidence give a head start on V(A). The investment-specific rules (group research, model stress testing, the 2024 cost disclosure, fact vs opinion, 7-year record guidance) are new.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
(1) Exercise **diligence, independence and thoroughness** when analysing investments, making recommendations and taking investment actions.
(2) Have a **reasonable and adequate basis**, supported by appropriate research and investigation.

How much diligence is enough depends on the investment's complexity, your role and the information available. A complex structured product needs far more work than an update on a blue-chip stock.

cards.title: Using others' research
cards.body:
You may rely on third-party or secondary research if you make reasonable efforts to check that it is sound. Review its assumptions, rigour, independence, timeliness and objectivity, and keep checking as long as you rely on it.

Relying on a credit rating or a well-known firm's report without understanding it isn't enough.

**Group research**: you may let your name appear on a team report you disagree with, if it has a reasonable basis. Document your dissent. You don't need to dissociate.

cards.title: Models and outside managers
cards.body:
**Quantitative models**: understand their assumptions and limits, and test them under a range of scenarios, including severe stress. Don't release a model you can't explain.

**External managers and sub-advisers**: do due diligence on their strategy, controls, compliance and performance record before hiring them, and keep monitoring afterwards.

A recommendation based on a rumour, a company's marketing presentation or a single conversation fails V(A).

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: This is close to IESBA's professional competence and due care, and to the auditor's idea of sufficient appropriate evidence. The difference is that CFA ties it to investment recommendations. Group reports, reliance on third-party research, stress testing models and selecting managers are all specific test topics.

lessons.title: V(B) Communication and V(C) Record Retention

cards.title: V(B): five duties
cards.body:
- (1) Disclose the **nature of the services** you provide and their **costs** to the client (added in 2024).
- (2) Disclose the basic format and general principles of your investment process, and promptly disclose **changes** that might materially affect it.
- (3) Disclose significant **limitations and risks** of the process.
- (4) Use reasonable judgement to identify the **important factors** and include them in communications.
- (5) **Distinguish fact from opinion**.

cards.title: Services and costs (2024)
cards.body:
Clients must understand what they will, and **won't**, receive, and the costs they'll bear: management and performance fees, trading costs and fund expenses. A written description in the client agreement is best practice.

“Reasonable detail” is enough. A fee stated as a percentage of assets doesn't have to be converted into a dollar amount in advance. Hidden or vague fees violate V(B)(1).

cards.title: Process, risks, fact vs opinion
cards.body:
Disclose material process changes promptly, such as moving from fundamental to quantitative stock selection, a key manager leaving, or adding leverage or derivatives.

Point out the main risks: liquidity, leverage, model limits.

Label forecasts as forecasts. “EPS will be $3.00” presents an opinion as fact. “We forecast EPS of $3.00” doesn't.

Short communications, such as posts or lists of recommendations, are fine if the fuller research is available.

cards.title: V(C) Record Retention
cards.body:
Develop and keep records that support your analyses, recommendations, actions and client communications: notes, models, emails, social-media messages.

Records are the **firm's property**. You can't take them when you leave, and you must recreate any analysis from public sources.

Where no regulation sets a period, CFA Institute recommends keeping records for at least **7 years**. If local law requires a different period, follow it.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: V(B)(5) catches forecasts stated with certainty. V(B)(2) catches undisclosed changes in strategy or key staff. V(C) is often tested with IV(A), when someone leaves with files. The 7-year figure is a **recommendation**, not a requirement of the Standard.

questions.stem: An analyst on a research committee disagrees with the team's Buy recommendation, but the team's process was thorough and its view is well supported. Her name appears on the report. Has she violated the Standards?
options: Yes, unless she removes her name.
No. She may document her dissent and stay on the report.
Yes, she has violated I(C), because the report doesn't reflect her opinion.
questions.explanation: A group report with a reasonable and adequate basis may carry the names of members who disagree. She should document her difference of opinion, but she doesn't need to dissociate. Her name on a well-founded group view is not a misrepresentation.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager buys mortgage-backed securities for clients relying only on their AAA ratings, without understanding how the securities are structured. Has she violated the Standards?
options: Yes, she has violated V(A).
No. Credit rating agencies are independent experts.
No, as long as the securities later perform well.
questions.explanation: V(A) requires a reasonable basis that fits the product's complexity. Relying on a rating alone, without understanding the structure, isn't diligent. Good later performance doesn't cure a lack of diligence at the time of the decision.

questions.stem: A quantitative analyst back-tests a new model only over the 2010–2019 bull market and then launches it for clients. Has he violated the Standards?
options: No. A decade of data is enough.
No, as long as clients are told the strategy is quantitative.
Yes. He failed to test the model under a range of scenarios, including stressed markets.
questions.explanation: V(A) guidance says models must be tested under a range of conditions, including severe downside scenarios. A sample of one benign market regime doesn't give a reasonable basis. Disclosing that the strategy is quantitative doesn't replace proper testing.

questions.stem: An analyst raises her rating on a stock after attending the company's investor-day presentation, without doing any other analysis. This most likely:
options: doesn't violate the Standards, because management is the best source of information.
violates V(A), because one company presentation isn't an adequate basis.
doesn't violate the Standards, because the presentation was public.
questions.explanation: Company presentations are promotional and one-sided. Changing a recommendation on that alone lacks independent, thorough analysis. The presentation being public settles the II(A) question, not the diligence question.

questions.stem: A research report states: “XYZ's earnings will grow 20% next year.” The figure comes from the analyst's model. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This violates V(B), because it fails to distinguish fact from opinion.
This isn't a violation if the model is reasonable.
This violates I(C) Misrepresentation only.
questions.explanation: A forecast is an opinion and must be presented as one, for example “we forecast…”. A reasonable model supports V(A) but doesn't fix the wording problem. V(B)(5) is the specific Standard that applies.

questions.stem: A firm switches its stock selection from fundamental analysis to a quantitative model. It tells clients six months later in its annual letter. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation, because the investment objective didn't change.
This isn't a violation, because an annual communication is sufficient.
This violates V(B). Material changes to the investment process must be disclosed promptly.
questions.explanation: A change from fundamental to quantitative selection is a material change to the investment process, and V(B)(2) requires prompt disclosure. An unchanged objective doesn't remove the need to disclose, and a six-month delay is not prompt.

questions.stem: An adviser's client agreement lists the services she provides but says only “standard fees apply”, with no other information about costs. Under the 2024 Standards, this is most likely:
options: not a violation, because clients can ask about fees.
a violation of V(B), which requires disclosure of the costs to the client.
not a violation, because only performance must be disclosed.
questions.explanation: Since 2024, V(B)(1) requires members to disclose the nature of their services and the costs clients will bear, in reasonable detail. “Standard fees apply” tells the client nothing. Expecting the client to ask is not disclosure.

questions.stem: Where no regulatory requirement applies, CFA Institute recommends keeping records that support investment recommendations for at least:
options: seven years
three years
as long as the client relationship lasts
questions.explanation: The V(C) guidance recommends at least seven years when no regulation sets a period. Local law that sets a different period takes precedence.

questions.stem: An analyst leaves her firm and wants to use, at her new employer, the research she produced at the old firm. What is she permitted to do?
options: Take copies, because she wrote the research herself.
Use the old reports after removing the former employer's name.
Recreate the research from public information and her own new work, without using the old firm's records.
questions.explanation: Records created at a firm belong to that firm (V(C), IV(A)). She can't take or reuse them, even if she wrote them, and removing the firm's name makes it worse by adding misrepresentation. She must rebuild the analysis independently.

questions.stem: An adviser's agreement sets her fee at 1% of assets under management per year. A client complains that he wasn't given a dollar estimate in advance. Has she violated V(B)?
options: No. Costs need only be disclosed in reasonable detail, and a percentage fee doesn't have to be converted into a dollar amount.
Yes. The dollar amount must be disclosed in advance.
Yes. Fees must be disclosed again after each year.
questions.explanation: The 2024 V(B)(1) guidance requires reasonable detail on costs. A clearly stated percentage-of-assets fee meets it, because the dollar amount depends on future asset values. Neither a dollar figure in advance nor annual re-disclosure is required.

questions.stem: The portfolio manager who designed and ran a firm's flagship strategy retires. The firm doesn't tell clients, because “the process is documented.” Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation, because the process is unchanged on paper.
This isn't a violation, because personnel changes are internal matters.
This violates V(B). A change in key personnel that could materially affect the process must be disclosed.
questions.explanation: V(B)(2) requires prompt disclosure of changes that might materially affect the investment process, including the loss of the key decision-maker. Having the process documented doesn't make the change immaterial to clients.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager has used an outside research provider for years. She learns that its lead analyst has left and that quality has slipped, but she keeps relying on its reports without review. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation, because the long relationship gives a reasonable basis.
This violates V(A). She must keep assessing whether third-party research is sound.
This isn't a violation, because responsibility for quality lies with the provider.
questions.explanation: V(A) requires reasonable efforts to confirm that third-party research is sound, and the checks must continue. Known warning signs call for a fresh review. A long relationship and the provider's own responsibility don't replace her diligence.

questions.stem: A fund uses three-times leverage and invests in thinly traded securities. Its marketing material describes the investment process but doesn't mention leverage or liquidity risk. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation if the fund's returns have been strong.
This violates V(B), because significant risks must be disclosed.
This violates III(D) Performance Presentation only.
questions.explanation: V(B)(3) requires disclosure of significant limitations and risks, and leverage and illiquidity are central ones here. Strong returns don't remove the duty. The material may also raise other issues, but the missing risk disclosure is a V(B) failure.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager hires a sub-adviser for emerging-market debt after one meeting and a single-page performance summary. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation, because the sub-adviser is responsible for its own compliance.
This isn't a violation, as long as the sub-adviser's returns are above average.
This most likely violates V(A), because selecting external managers requires due diligence.
questions.explanation: V(A) requires reviewing an outside manager's strategy, controls, compliance and the reliability of its performance figures before hiring. One meeting and a summary sheet aren't enough. The sub-adviser's own duties don't replace the manager's.

questions.stem: An analyst records her research in a personal notebook and throws it away after her report is published. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This violates V(C). She must keep records supporting her recommendation.
This isn't a violation, because the published report is the record.
This isn't a violation, as long as she can remember the analysis.
questions.explanation: V(C) requires keeping the records that support a recommendation, such as notes, models and sources. The published report shows the conclusion, not the basis for it. Memory is not a record.

flashcards.back: (1) Diligence, independence and thoroughness. (2) A reasonable and adequate basis supported by research. The depth needed depends on complexity and role.
You may keep your name on it if the report has a reasonable basis. Document your dissent. You don't need to dissociate.
(1) Nature of services and costs (2024) · (2) investment process and prompt notice of changes · (3) significant limitations and risks · (4) important factors · (5) fact vs opinion.
Reasonable detail. A % of AUM fee need not be converted to a dollar amount in advance. Say what services are and aren't included.
At least 7 years if no regulation applies (a recommendation). Otherwise follow local law. Records belong to the firm.
Understand the assumptions and limits, and test across scenarios including severe stress before relying on the model.

modules.title: Guidance for Standard VI: Conflicts of Interest
modules.summary: VI(A) avoid conflicts where reasonably possible, otherwise disclose them prominently in plain language (2024); VI(B) clients and employer trade before you; VI(C) disclose referral fees before the engagement.

acca.note: IESBA threats and safeguards (self-interest and others) give the general idea. The CFA specifics are new: what to disclose and to whom, beneficial ownership, front-running, family accounts and referral-fee disclosure.

cards.title: The rule (2024)
cards.body:
**Avoid** conflicts, or make **full and fair disclosure** of everything that could reasonably be expected to impair your independence and objectivity, or interfere with your duties to clients, prospective clients and your employer.

Disclosures must be **prominent**, in **plain language**, and must actually communicate the information. Avoidance is preferred where it is reasonably possible. Disclosure is the fallback, not a fig leaf.

cards.title: Common conflicts and who to tell
rows: Board seat at a company you cover or invest in
Clients; employer (plus IV(B) consent if paid)
Firm's investment-banking or market-making relationship with the issuer
Pay incentives (e.g., bonus for selling in-house products)
Personal holdings that could affect your work

cards.title: What full and fair means
cards.body:
Disclosure buried in the fine print of a 40-page document, or written in legal jargon, fails the 2024 test. Give enough detail for clients to judge the conflict: what it is, how big it is where relevant, and how it might affect your advice.

Even a small holding may need disclosure if a reasonable person would see a conflict. Disclosure doesn't cure everything: some conduct, such as front-running, is prohibited outright.

cards.title: Conflicts across departments
cards.body:
A broker-dealer's analyst covers a company whose bond issue the firm is underwriting. The firm should use firewalls, consider restricting research or putting the issuer on a restricted list, and disclose the banking relationship prominently in any report it does publish.

An analyst who inherits shares in a company she covers should disclose this to her employer and clients, or avoid the conflict by selling the shares or handing over coverage.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: The IESBA approach is to identify threats (self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, intimidation), evaluate them, and apply safeguards or decline. The 2024 CFA rule is similar in spirit: avoid where reasonably possible, otherwise disclose prominently and plainly. CFA questions test **what** must be disclosed and **to whom**, not the names of threat categories.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
Investment transactions for **clients and employers** must take priority over transactions in which you are a **beneficial owner**. The order is clients → employer → you.

You may invest for yourself, but never ahead of clients or to their disadvantage, and never by exploiting knowledge of client orders or pending recommendations. Trading ahead of them is **front-running**.

cards.title: Beneficial ownership
cards.body:
You are a beneficial owner if you have a direct or indirect financial interest: your own accounts, joint accounts, your spouse's or dependent children's accounts, and accounts you control, such as a family trust.

**Family accounts that are regular fee-paying client accounts** must be treated like any other client. Don't favour them, and don't disadvantage them, for example by leaving them out of IPO allocations.

cards.title: Firm procedures
cards.body:
- **Pre-clearance** of personal trades by compliance
- **Blackout or restricted periods** around client trades and research releases
- Limited participation in **IPOs** (many firms ban hot IPOs) and pre-approval of **private placements**
- **Reporting**: duplicate trade confirmations and periodic holdings reports
- Disclosure of the firm's personal-trading policy to clients

These are recommended procedures. The requirement itself is the priority rule.

cards.title: Front-running
cards.body:
Mei, a portfolio manager, decides to buy 500,000 shares of Alpha for her clients. That morning she buys 2,000 shares for herself, then executes the client order, which pushes the price up 3%. She has violated VI(B) by trading ahead of her clients.

If she had bought only after the client order was fully executed, without exploiting it, there would be no violation, subject to firm policy.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: VI(B) doesn't ban personal trading, or owning what clients own. It bans **trading first** and **taking advantage** of client trades. Selling your own shares before releasing a Sell recommendation is a classic violation, and it also breaches II(A) if the rating is MNPI.

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
Disclose to your **employer, clients and prospective clients**, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration or benefit you receive from, or pay to, others for recommending products or services.

Disclose **before** the client enters into any formal agreement for the service. The client can then judge any bias in your recommendation and the true cost of the service.

cards.title: What counts
cards.body:
Cash fees, a share of fees, reciprocal referrals, free research or services, and gifts given in return for referrals all count. The rule covers referral payments **received** and **paid**, and **internal** referral bonuses within your own firm, for example a bank adviser rewarded for steering clients to the private-banking unit.

Disclose the **nature** and the **value**. A reasonable estimate of the value is fine.

cards.title: Reciprocal referral
cards.body:
A financial planner sends clients to an estate lawyer, and the lawyer sends clients back to the planner. No money changes hands.

This is still a referral arrangement. The planner must disclose it to her employer and to the clients and prospects she refers, because the referrals she expects in return give her an incentive.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: VI(C) requires **disclosure**, not consent and not refusal. If the member disclosed the nature and value to the client before the engagement, there is no violation. Compare IV(B), which needs written consent, and I(B), which may require declining.

questions.stem: An analyst owns a small number of shares in a company she rates Buy. Local law doesn't require disclosure, and she doesn't disclose the holding. Has she violated the Standards?
options: No. The holding is small.
Yes, she has violated VI(A).
No. The law doesn't require disclosure.
questions.explanation: Owning shares in a company you recommend is a conflict a reasonable person would expect to affect objectivity. She must avoid it or disclose it. Under I(A), the stricter Standard applies even when local law is silent, and a small holding doesn't remove the conflict.

questions.stem: A firm discloses its market-making in the stocks it recommends in a footnote set in tiny type at the end of a 50-page report, written in legal jargon. Has the firm complied with VI(A)?
options: Yes. The conflict has been disclosed.
Yes. Market-making is not a conflict of interest.
No. Disclosure must be prominent and in plain language.
questions.explanation: Since 2024, VI(A) requires disclosure that is prominent, in plain language and effective. A buried, jargon-filled footnote fails that test. Market-making in a recommended stock is a conflict that must be disclosed.

questions.stem: Which approach to a conflict of interest is most consistent with Standard VI(A) as revised in 2024?
options: Avoid the conflict where reasonably possible. If that isn't possible, disclose it prominently and in plain language.
Disclose the conflict, which is always sufficient.
Get written approval from CFA Institute before acting.
questions.explanation: The 2024 wording, “Avoid or Disclose Conflicts”, prefers avoidance and allows effective disclosure as the fallback. Disclosure isn't automatically enough, especially if it is buried or vague. CFA Institute doesn't approve individual conflicts.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager's bonus depends partly on sales of her firm's in-house funds. She recommends them to clients without mentioning the bonus. Has she violated the Standards?
options: Yes, she has violated VI(A), because her pay arrangement is a conflict that must be disclosed or avoided.
No, as long as the in-house funds are suitable.
No, because her employer approved the pay scheme.
questions.explanation: Incentive pay that rewards recommending particular products could reasonably be expected to impair objectivity. Clients must be told, or the conflict avoided. Suitability is a separate requirement, and the employer's approval doesn't replace disclosure to clients.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager decides to sell a stock across all client accounts. Before entering the client orders, he sells his own shares. Has he violated the Standards?
options: No, as long as he discloses the sale later.
Yes, he has violated VI(B).
No, if his sale is small relative to the client trades.
questions.explanation: Client transactions must come before personal ones. Selling first gives him a better price at clients' expense, which is front-running. Later disclosure doesn't cure it, and the size of his trade doesn't matter.

questions.stem: An analyst's sister has a fee-paying account at the firm, and a hot IPO suits her. The analyst allocates her shares pro rata like all other eligible clients. Has the analyst violated the Standards?
options: Yes. Family accounts must be excluded from IPOs.
Yes, unless the sister gives up her allocation.
No, the analyst has not violated the Standards.
questions.explanation: A family member's fee-paying account is a client account and should be treated like other client accounts, neither favoured nor disadvantaged. A pro rata allocation does that. There is no rule excluding such accounts. This assumes the analyst has no beneficial interest in the account.

questions.stem: An analyst buys shares for her personal account in a company her firm doesn't cover and that no client holds. She follows the firm's pre-clearance procedure. Has she violated the Standards?
options: No, she has not violated the Standards.
Yes. Personal trades must be approved by clients.
Yes. Members may not trade individual stocks.
questions.explanation: VI(B) doesn't ban personal investing. It requires that client and employer trades come first and that clients aren't disadvantaged. With no client interest involved and pre-clearance followed, there is no conflict. Client approval isn't required.

questions.stem: Which procedure most directly prevents violations of VI(B)?
options: Pro rata allocation of block trades among client accounts
Pre-clearance of personal trades, with blackout periods around client trades
Keeping records for seven years
questions.explanation: Pre-clearance and blackout periods stop members trading ahead of clients, which is the core of VI(B). Pro rata allocation addresses fairness between clients under III(B). Record retention is the V(C) recommendation.

questions.stem: An adviser receives $200 for each client he refers to an accounting firm. He tells clients about it only if they ask, after they have hired the accountant. Has he violated the Standards?
options: No. He disclosed the fee when asked.
No. The fee is small.
Yes. He must disclose before the client enters into an agreement for the service.
questions.explanation: VI(C) requires proactive disclosure of the nature and value of referral compensation before the engagement, so the client can weigh the recommendation. Disclosing only when asked, and afterwards, is too late. The size of the fee doesn't matter.

questions.stem: A financial planner and an estate lawyer refer clients to each other. No money changes hands. Under VI(C), the planner must:
options: disclose the reciprocal referral arrangement.
do nothing, because no cash is involved.
end the arrangement, because reciprocal referrals are prohibited.
questions.explanation: Referral benefits include non-cash consideration such as reciprocal referrals. The planner must disclose the arrangement to her employer and to the clients and prospects concerned. VI(C) requires disclosure, not ending the arrangement.

questions.stem: A charterholder at a bank receives an internal bonus for each client he refers to the bank's brokerage unit. Which statement is most accurate?
options: No disclosure is needed, because the payment comes from within his own firm.
He must disclose the referral pay to the clients he refers.
He must refuse the bonus.
questions.explanation: Referral compensation inside a firm is still compensation for recommending a service, and clients should know about it. VI(C) requires disclosure, not refusal.

questions.stem: A member receives a referral fee. Before the engagement, she discloses its nature and approximate value to the client in writing, and her employer knows about the arrangement. Has she violated the Standards?
options: Yes. She also needed the client's written consent.
Yes. Referral fees above a nominal value are prohibited.
No, she has not violated the Standards.
questions.explanation: VI(C) is met by timely disclosure of the nature and value of the fee to the employer, clients and prospects as appropriate. The Standard doesn't require client consent or cap the size of fees.

questions.stem: An analyst learns that her firm will shortly issue a Buy recommendation on a stock. She tells her husband, who buys the stock for his own account before the report is released. Has a violation occurred?
options: Yes. She is a beneficial owner of her spouse's account, and it traded ahead of clients.
No. The account belongs to her husband.
No. The recommendation hadn't been released yet.
questions.explanation: A spouse's account is normally one in which the member has beneficial ownership, so VI(B) applies, and the pending recommendation may also be MNPI under II(A). Trading before release is exactly what the Standards prohibit.

questions.stem: An analyst who covers a company is offered a seat on its board. Which action is most consistent with the 2024 version of VI(A)?
options: Accept the seat and keep covering the company, because disclosure always suffices.
Decline the seat, or hand over coverage of the company, because avoiding the conflict is preferred where reasonably possible.
Accept the seat only if it is unpaid, because unpaid seats raise no conflict.
questions.explanation: Under the 2024 wording, avoidance is preferred where reasonably possible, and here it plainly is. Disclosure isn't always sufficient. An unpaid board seat still creates duties to that company that conflict with objective research.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager gets an allocation of a hot IPO for his personal account from the broker that handles his clients' trades. His clients would have wanted the shares. Has he violated the Standards?
options: No. The broker allocated the shares to him personally.
No, as long as he pre-clears the trade with compliance afterwards.
Yes, he has violated VI(B).
questions.explanation: Taking scarce IPO shares for himself while his clients go without puts his interests ahead of theirs. It may also be a broker inducement (I(B)). Pre-clearance after the trade is meaningless, and who allocated the shares doesn't change the conflict.

questions.stem: A member receives referral fees from a hedge fund for steering clients to it. She discloses the fees to her clients but not to her employer. Has she violated the Standards?
options: Yes. Her employer must also be told.
No. Clients are the ones affected.
No, if the fees are paid to her personally outside work.
questions.explanation: VI(C) requires disclosure to the employer, clients and prospective clients as appropriate. Referral fees affect the employer too, for example by influencing which products she recommends. Personal payment makes disclosure to the employer more important, not less.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager executes trades for the firm's proprietary account before client orders in the same security. Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation, because VI(B) restricts only the member's personal trades.
This isn't a violation if the proprietary account is disclosed.
This is a violation, because client transactions take priority over the employer's.
questions.explanation: The order of priority is clients, then employer, then the member. Trading the firm's account ahead of clients puts the employer first, which breaches the duty of loyalty to clients under III(A). VI(B) itself names transactions for clients and employers. Disclosing the account doesn't permit trading ahead of clients.

questions.stem: A charterholder owns 1% of a small company and plans to recommend it to clients. Which course of action is least appropriate?
options: Disclose the ownership prominently in the recommendation.
Recommend it and mention the ownership only if a client asks.
Avoid the conflict by not recommending the company.
questions.explanation: VI(A) requires avoidance or full, fair and prominent disclosure. Disclosing only on request isn't full and fair. Both prominent disclosure and avoidance are acceptable, and avoidance is preferred under the 2024 wording.

flashcards.back: Avoid conflicts where reasonably possible. Otherwise disclose them fully and fairly, prominently, in plain language, to clients, prospects and the employer as relevant.
Clients → employer → you (beneficial owner).
A direct or indirect financial interest: your own, joint, spouse's and dependent children's accounts, and accounts you control.
Treat it like any other client: don't favour it, don't exclude it (e.g., from IPOs).
Pre-clearance, blackout periods, limits on IPOs and private placements, duplicate confirmations and holdings reports, disclosure of the policy.
Nature and value of any referral benefit (cash, services, reciprocal referrals, internal bonuses) → to employer, clients and prospects → before the engagement.
VI(A): avoid where reasonably possible, otherwise disclose. VI(C): disclose. IV(B): written consent. I(B): decline gifts that could compromise you. I(A): dissociate.

modules.title: Guidance for Standard VII: Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate
modules.summary: VII(A) protect the integrity of CFA Institute programs (no cheating, no disclosing exam content, no false statements); VII(B) refer to the CFA designation, membership and candidacy accurately.

acca.note: ACCA also limits use of its designatory letters to members in good standing. The CFA's specific rules on exam confidentiality, candidate status and correct use of the mark are new and heavily tested.

lessons.title: VII(A) Conduct in CFA Institute Programs

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
Don't do anything that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation, or the integrity, validity or security of CFA Institute programs, including the CFA Program and CIPM.

This applies to candidates and members alike, including members who volunteer as graders, question writers or committee members.

cards.title: Typical violations
cards.body:
- Cheating, or helping someone cheat. Using unauthorised notes or aids.
- Breaking testing rules, for example writing after time is called.
- Disclosing **confidential exam content**: specific questions, or which topics or formulas were or were not tested.
- Giving false information to CFA Institute, for example on the Professional Conduct Statement, an application, or about work experience.
- Volunteers leaking confidential grading or question material.

cards.title: What's allowed
cards.body:
You may express **opinions** about the exam, the curriculum or CFA Institute policies, even harsh ones such as “the exam was too long” or “the pass rate is unfair”.

You may discuss curriculum topics in study groups **before** the exam, and say you found it hard.

The line is anything that reveals what was **on**, or **not on**, your exam.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Post-exam social-media scenarios are common. “Glad I memorised the duration formula, it came up twice!” is a violation because it reveals tested content. “Brutal exam, glad it's over” is fine. “There was nothing on the X model” is also a violation, because content that was **not** tested is confidential too.

lessons.title: VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute and the CFA designation

cards.title: The rule
cards.body:
When you refer to CFA Institute, membership, the CFA designation or candidacy, don't misrepresent or exaggerate what it means or implies.

You may describe the program factually: three levels, rigorous, a commitment to ethics. You may **not** claim that charterholders or candidates achieve **superior** performance, or that the designation **guarantees** anything.

cards.title: Who can say what
cards.body:
- **Charterholder** (“CFA” after your name): you passed all levels, met the work-experience requirement and became a member, **and** you currently pay dues and file the annual PCS. If membership lapses, stop using the designation until you are reinstated.
- **Candidate**: only while you are registered for an upcoming exam or awaiting results.
- **No partial designation**: “CFA Level II” and “CFA (expected 2027)” are prohibited.
- Factual statements are fine, e.g., “passed Level II of the CFA Program” or “passed all three levels on the first attempt” if true.

cards.title: Right vs wrong usage
rows: Jane Smith, a CFA · Jane Smith, C.F.A.
Level II candidate in the CFA Program
CFA Level II candidate · CFA Level II
Passed all three levels on the first attempt (if true)
Passed with the highest scores · charterholders earn superior returns

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: ACCA also restricts use of “ACCA” to members in good standing. The CFA rules are tested on tiny wording differences: “CFA” is an **adjective**, never a noun or plural. There is no partial or “expected” designation. Claims that the charter brings superior returns are misrepresentation.

questions.stem: After the exam, a candidate posts: “Can't believe there was nothing at all on put–call parity.” Has the candidate violated the Standards?
options: No. She revealed only what was not on the exam.
No. She didn't disclose a specific question.
Yes, the candidate has violated VII(A).
questions.explanation: Confidential exam information includes the topics and formulas that were or were not tested. Revealing that a topic was missing helps future candidates and compromises exam integrity.

questions.stem: A candidate posts online: “The exam was much harder than I expected, and CFA Institute should publish more practice questions.” Has the candidate violated the Standards?
options: Yes. Candidates may not comment publicly on the exam.
No, the candidate has not violated the Standards.
Yes. Criticising CFA Institute damages its reputation.
questions.explanation: Candidates may give opinions about the exam's difficulty and about CFA Institute policies, including criticism. VII(A) is breached only by revealing confidential content or otherwise undermining the program's integrity.

questions.stem: A member's application to CFA Institute claims four years of portfolio-management experience when he has only two. Which Standard has he most directly violated?
options: VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs
VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program
IV(A) Loyalty
questions.explanation: Giving false information to CFA Institute, such as overstating work experience, undermines the integrity of its programs, which is VII(A). VII(B) concerns how members describe the designation to others. Loyalty to an employer isn't involved.

questions.stem: A candidate keeps writing his answer after the proctor calls time. Has he violated the Standards?
options: No, as long as he had already decided on his answer.
No, unless he wrote for more than a minute.
Yes, he has violated VII(A).
questions.explanation: Breaking testing rules, including writing after time is called, compromises the integrity of the exam. There is no allowance for a short overrun or for an answer already decided.

questions.stem: A candidate's résumé reads “John Lee, CFA Level III candidate”. Is this acceptable?
options: No. It implies a partial designation. It should say “Level III candidate in the CFA Program”.
Yes. It is accurate if he is registered for Level III.
Yes, provided he passes Level III.
questions.explanation: “CFA Level III” attaches the mark to a level, suggesting a partial designation, which is prohibited. Candidates may correctly describe themselves as candidates in the CFA Program if they are registered or awaiting results.

questions.stem: A charterholder hasn't paid her dues or filed her Professional Conduct Statement for two years, but still puts “CFA” on her business cards. Has she violated the Standards?
options: No. A designation, once earned, is permanent.
Yes. She must stop using the designation until her membership is reinstated.
No, as long as she completes continuing-education hours.
questions.explanation: The right to use the CFA designation depends on current membership: dues paid and an annual PCS filed. Once membership lapses, she must stop using it until she is reinstated. Continuing education is not the condition.

questions.stem: A firm's brochure says: “Our CFA charterholders achieve better returns than non-charterholder managers because of their training.” Which statement is most accurate?
options: This violates VII(B).
This isn't a violation if the firm's data supports it.
This isn't a violation, because it refers to the firm rather than an individual.
questions.explanation: Claiming or implying that the designation leads to superior investment performance exaggerates what the charter means, which VII(B) prohibits. The firm's own data doesn't make it acceptable, and VII(B) applies to firm materials prepared by members.

questions.stem: A candidate passed Level I in February 2026 and has not registered for Level II. Her LinkedIn profile says “CFA Program candidate”. Is this acceptable?
options: Yes. She is enrolled in the program.
Yes, for 12 months after passing.
No. She is not currently a candidate.
questions.explanation: A person is a candidate only while registered for an upcoming exam or awaiting results. She may say factually that she passed Level I, but not that she is currently a candidate. There is no 12-month grace period.

questions.stem: Which statement is acceptable under VII(B)?
options: “I am a CFA.”
“I passed all three levels of the CFA exam on my first attempt.” (true)
“John Smith, CFA (expected 2028)”
questions.explanation: A true, factual statement of exam history is allowed. “CFA” must not be used as a noun, and an “expected” designation implies a partial charter, which is prohibited.

questions.stem: Lina has passed all three levels but hasn't yet completed the work-experience requirement, so the charter hasn't been awarded. How may she describe herself?
options: She may use “CFA (pending)” after her name.
She may say she has passed all three levels, but she may not use the designation until it is awarded.
She may use “CFA”, because passing the exams is the main requirement.
questions.explanation: The designation may be used only once it has been awarded, which requires work experience and membership as well as the exams. A factual statement about passing the exams is fine. “Pending” implies a partial designation.

questions.stem: A member who volunteers as an exam grader describes on his blog, without naming it, how a particular constructed-response question was graded. Has he violated the Standards?
options: No. He didn't name the question.
No. Grading methods are public knowledge.
Yes, he has violated VII(A).
questions.explanation: Volunteers must keep exam and grading information confidential. Describing how a specific question was graded compromises exam security, even without naming it. Grading guidelines are not public.

questions.stem: Before the exam, a study group shares notes and a prep provider's practice questions with one another. Has anyone violated the Standards?
options: No, no one has violated the Standards.
Yes. Discussing the curriculum before the exam violates VII(A).
Yes. Sharing prep material compromises exam security.
questions.explanation: Studying together and sharing legitimately obtained study material before the exam is fine. VII(A) concerns actual exam content, cheating and testing rules. Copyright on prep material is a separate matter, not a breach of exam security.

questions.stem: A charterholder's marketing material says: “As a CFA charterholder, I am committed to high ethical standards.” Is this acceptable?
options: Yes. It is an acceptable statement.
No. It implies superiority over non-charterholders.
No. Only CFA Institute may make statements about ethics.
questions.explanation: Charterholders may say they are committed to the Code and Standards and to high ethical conduct, because that is what the designation requires. The statement makes no claim about superior performance.

questions.stem: Marcus, CFA, names his new advisory firm “CFA Wealth Partners”. Is this acceptable?
options: Yes, because he is a charterholder.
Yes, provided all of the firm's advisers are charterholders.
No. It is an improper use of the CFA mark.
questions.explanation: The CFA mark may be used only as an individual's designation, never as part of a firm name. Being a charterholder, or employing only charterholders, doesn't permit it.

questions.stem: After sitting the exam, a candidate tells friends who are taking it in a later window: “Make sure you know the mechanics of the dividend discount model. There were lots of questions on it.” Which statement is most accurate?
options: This isn't a violation, because they will sit a different version of the exam.
This violates VII(A).
This isn't a violation, because the dividend discount model is a broad curriculum topic.
questions.explanation: Revealing which topics were heavily tested is disclosing confidential exam information. It gives later candidates an unfair advantage, which is exactly the harm VII(A) prevents. A different version or a broad topic doesn't make it acceptable.

flashcards.back: Cheating, breaking testing rules, revealing questions or which topics and formulas were or were not tested, false statements to CFA Institute (PCS, applications, work experience), volunteers leaking grading information.
Opinions and criticism of the exam, curriculum or CFA Institute policy. Pre-exam study discussions. “It was hard.”

flashcards.front: Conditions for using “CFA” after your name
flashcards.back: Charter awarded (exams, experience, membership) and currently a member in good standing: dues paid and annual PCS filed.

flashcards.front: Who is a CFA Program candidate?
flashcards.back: Someone registered for an upcoming exam or awaiting results. Not someone who passed a level and hasn't registered for the next.
An adjective, never a noun or plural. No partial designation (“CFA Level II”) and no “expected” charter. Not in a firm name. No claims of superior returns.

modules.title: Application of the Code and Standards: Level I
modules.summary: Putting it together: a method for any ethics question, telling neighbouring Standards apart, requirements vs recommended procedures, and multi-issue cases like those on the exam.

acca.note: This LM applies all seven CFA Standards to cases. ACCA ethics practice helps with the habit of judgement, but the rules applied are CFA-specific.

cards.title: A method for any ethics question
cards.body:
- (1) **Who** is acting? A member or candidate? Non-members aren't bound.
- (2) **Whose interest** is at stake: client, employer, market or CFA Institute?
- (3) Which Standard group fits, and then which sub-standard?
- (4) Was the **requirement** met, not just best practice? Check timing (before or after), form (written or verbal) and who was told.
- (5) Choose the answer that matches the Standard's exact remedy: disclose, get consent, decline, dissociate or don't act.

cards.title: Neighbouring Standards
rows: One client vs another / clients vs your own account
Basis is inside information (prohibited) / basis is inadequate research
Employer's confidential information / client's confidential information
Accepting things that compromise you / disclosing or avoiding conflicts you have
Integrity of the exam and program / how you describe the CFA designation

cards.title: Which remedy does each Standard require?
rows: VI(A) conflicts, VI(C) referral fees, V(B) services, costs, process and risks, issuer-paid research, client gifts to the employer
I(B) lavish or influencing gifts, I(E) work beyond your competence, VI(A) where reasonably possible
Don't act or cause others to act

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Distractors are often the right Standard with the wrong remedy, such as “disclose” where written consent was needed, or the right remedy at the wrong time, such as disclosing after the fact. Read the last line of the stem first, so you know whether it asks “violation?”, “which Standard?” or “best action?”.

cards.title: Must vs should
cards.body:
Each Standard has a **requirement**, which you violate if you fail it, and **recommended procedures**, which are best practice: skipping them is not a violation on its own.

Questions often ask “which is required?” or “which is the best practice?”. Common examples of recommended-only items: GIPS compliance under III(D), 7-year record retention under V(C), firewalls under II(A), and written allocation policies under III(B).

cards.title: Recommended procedures by Standard
rows: Firm code of ethics, compliance procedures, keeping staff informed of laws
Gift policies, firewalls, restricted lists, analysts' pay not tied to banking deals
Firewalls, watch and restricted lists, monitoring of trades
Written allocation policy, simultaneous dissemination, recording order times
Written IPS, reviewed at least annually
Keep records for at least 7 years where no law applies

cards.title: Firm vs individual
cards.body:
Many procedures are the **firm's** job, such as a code of ethics or a compliance manual. An individual member doesn't violate the Standards just because the firm lacks one. A **supervisor** who accepts responsibility without adequate procedures does (IV(C)).

Individuals must still meet the Standard itself. Having no written allocation policy doesn't excuse an unfair allocation.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: If an answer says something is “required by the Standards”, be suspicious when it refers to GIPS compliance, specific continuing-education hours, 7-year retention, or reporting violations to regulators or CFA Institute. These are recommended or encouraged, not required.

cards.title: Case 1: The departing star
cards.body:
Leo, CFA, a portfolio manager at Firm A, plans to start his own firm. While still employed he:
- registers the new firm: **allowed**
- tells clients over lunch they're welcome to follow him: **IV(A) violation** (solicitation)
- copies his model files to a personal drive: **IV(A) and V(C) violation**

After leaving, he calls former clients from memory, with no non-compete in place: **allowed**. His marketing shows Firm A's track record as his new firm's without disclosure: **III(D) violation**.

cards.title: Case 2: The busy analyst
cards.body:
Sara, CFA, covers RetailCo.
- She owns RetailCo shares, and her report discloses this prominently: **VI(A) met**.
- The company flies her to a new store on its corporate jet, although commercial flights exist: **I(B) violation**.
- The CFO privately hints that sales are far below consensus. That is MNPI, so she must not act and should urge public disclosure: **II(A)**.
- Her report says “EPS will be $2.10”: **V(B)** fact vs opinion.

cards.title: Case 3: IPO week
cards.body:
Firm B gets a small allocation of a hot IPO. Pat, CFA:
- gives it all to his 10 largest clients: **III(B) violation**. It should be pro rata across all clients for whom it is suitable.
- keeps 100 shares for his own account: **VI(B) violation** (and III(B))

His supervisor learns of this, accepts Pat's apology and does nothing more: **IV(C) violation**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Level I ethics questions are stand-alone, each with a short scenario. Often the member did several things and only one is a violation, so first eliminate the options that describe compliant behaviour. When two Standards seem to apply, choose the one whose specific wording matches the conduct.

questions.stem: An analyst sells her personal shares in a company the day before her firm releases her Sell rating on it. Which Standard most directly addresses this?
options: III(B) Fair Dealing
VI(B) Priority of Transactions
V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis
questions.explanation: Trading her own account ahead of the clients who will act on the rating is a priority-of-transactions problem. The unreleased rating may also be MNPI. III(B) concerns fairness between clients, and V(A) concerns the quality of the research.

questions.stem: A manager sends new research recommendations to his premium clients a day before all other clients. Which Standard most directly addresses this?
options: III(B) Fair Dealing
VI(B) Priority of Transactions
III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
questions.explanation: Favouring one group of clients over another in the timing of recommendations is a fair-dealing issue. VI(B) concerns personal trades against clients. III(A) is the broader duty of loyalty, but III(B) is the specific Standard.

questions.stem: An employee gives details of his employer's proprietary trading algorithm to a competitor. Which Standard most directly addresses this?
options: III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality
II(A) Material Nonpublic Information
IV(A) Loyalty
questions.explanation: Revealing the employer's confidential information harms the employer, which is IV(A). III(E) protects client information, not the employer's trade secrets. II(A) concerns trading on material nonpublic information about investments.

questions.stem: A client offers a portfolio manager a performance bonus. The manager tells his employer about it verbally and then accepts. What was deficient in his conduct?
options: He also needed to disclose the bonus to all his other clients.
He should have declined, because client bonuses are prohibited.
The consent needed to be in writing.
questions.explanation: IV(B) requires written consent from all parties before accepting compensation that could conflict with the employer's interest. Client bonuses aren't banned, and the Standard doesn't require disclosure to every other client.

questions.stem: Which of the following is required by the Standards, rather than merely recommended?
options: Complying with GIPS
Making reasonable efforts to ensure that performance information is fair, accurate and complete
Keeping records for at least seven years
questions.explanation: III(D) requires fair, accurate and complete performance information. GIPS compliance is the recommended way to achieve it. The seven-year retention period is a recommendation that applies when no regulation sets one.

questions.stem: A member's firm has no written trade-allocation policy, but the member allocates all block trades fairly, pro rata. Has the member violated the Standards?
options: No. The requirement is fair dealing, and a written policy is only recommended.
Yes. III(B) requires a written allocation policy.
Yes. He must not trade until a written policy exists.
questions.explanation: The III(B) requirement is to deal fairly with all clients. Written allocation procedures are a recommended practice. Because his allocations are fair, he complies.

questions.stem: Which statement about reporting violations is most accurate?
options: Members must report all suspected violations to the regulator.
Members are encouraged, but not required, to report suspected violations by others to CFA Institute.
Members must report all suspected violations by other members to CFA Institute.
questions.explanation: The Standards require members to dissociate from violations they know of. They encourage reporting to CFA Institute or regulators but don't require it, unless local law does.

questions.stem: Which is a recommended procedure for complying with III(C) Suitability?
options: Preparing a written IPS and reviewing it at least annually
Allocating IPO shares pro rata
Pre-clearing personal trades
questions.explanation: A written IPS, reviewed regularly, is the main recommended procedure for suitability. Pro rata allocation supports III(B), and pre-clearance supports VI(B).

questions.stem: Leo, CFA, plans to leave his firm and start a competing one. Which of his actions violated the Standards?
options: Registering his new firm while still employed
Contacting former clients from memory after leaving, with no non-compete in place
Inviting clients to follow him while he was still employed
questions.explanation: Soliciting clients while still employed violates IV(A). Preparations such as registering a firm are allowed, and contacting former clients from memory after leaving is allowed when no non-compete applies.

questions.stem: Sara, CFA, owns RetailCo shares, and her firm's policy permits holdings that are disclosed. Her report discloses the holding in plain language on the first page. She also flew to a RetailCo store on the company's jet, although commercial flights were available. Which of her actions violated the Standards?
options: Owning RetailCo shares while covering the company
Accepting the corporate jet when commercial flights were available
Disclosing her ownership in the report
questions.explanation: Under I(B), issuer-provided travel is acceptable only when no commercial option exists. Her prominent, plain-language disclosure meets VI(A), so the holding itself isn't a violation. Disclosure is what the Standards ask for.
