questions.stem: Ana, a CFA Program candidate at an asset manager, is told by her supervisor to allocate a block trade only to accounts that pay performance fees. What should she do?
options: Follow the instruction, because of her duty of loyalty to her employer.
Follow the instruction, and disclose the policy to the other clients afterwards.
Refuse, allocate pro rata to all accounts that ordered, and escalate to compliance if pressed.
questions.explanation: Fair dealing with clients (III(B)) comes before following an employer's instruction. Loyalty to the employer never requires harming clients. Disclosing afterwards doesn't fix an unfair allocation, and Ana must dissociate from it under I(A).

questions.stem: Which of the following situations is not a violation of the Standards?
options: A member offers premium research, disclosed to all clients, to clients who pay higher fees.
A member buys shares for her personal account ahead of client orders.
A member accepts a client's bonus for beating the benchmark, with verbal approval from his boss.
questions.explanation: Disclosed premium service tiers that are open to all clients are consistent with III(B). Trading ahead of clients violates VI(B). A client performance bonus needs written consent under IV(B), so verbal approval isn't enough.

questions.stem: Kim, CFA, an analyst at a broker-dealer, covers a company for which her firm is underwriting a share issue. Her Buy rating is supported by her own analysis. The report prominently discloses the underwriting relationship and states that her pay isn't tied to investment banking. Has Kim most likely violated the Standards?
options: No, she has most likely not violated the Standards.
Yes. She has violated I(B), because analysts may not cover their firm's banking clients.
Yes. Under the 2024 Standards, disclosure is no longer an acceptable way to handle conflicts.
questions.explanation: Her rating has a reasonable basis, her pay is independent of banking, and the conflict is disclosed prominently and in plain language, which satisfies I(B) and VI(A). Analysts may cover banking clients if they stay independent. The 2024 rule prefers avoidance where reasonably possible but still accepts effective disclosure.

questions.stem: Tom, CFA, manages a company's pension plan. The company's CFO asks him to buy the company's own shares for the plan to support the share price during a hostile takeover attempt, and Tom does so. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Tom hasn't violated the Standards, because the sponsoring company is his client.
Tom hasn't violated the Standards, as long as the shares fit within the plan's guidelines.
Tom has violated III(A), because his duty is owed to plan participants and beneficiaries.
questions.explanation: A pension manager's loyalty is owed to the participants and beneficiaries. Buying shares to protect management from a takeover serves the sponsor, not the beneficiaries. Fitting within the guidelines doesn't make a purchase for that purpose loyal or prudent.

questions.stem: Rita, a CFA Program candidate and research assistant, is told to put her name on a report whose key assumptions her supervisor made up without any supporting analysis. What should she do?
options: Sign it, because group research may carry her name even if she disagrees.
Refuse to have her name on the report, because it lacks a reasonable basis.
Sign it, and add a footnote saying she disagrees.
questions.explanation: The group-research allowance applies only when the report has a reasonable and adequate basis. A report built on unsupported assumptions fails V(A), so she must dissociate under I(A). A footnote doesn't cure a report with no reasonable basis.

questions.stem: Hans, CFA, receives access to a research database from a broker in return for sending client trades to that broker. He uses the database in managing client portfolios. The broker's execution is competitive, and the arrangement is disclosed. Has Hans violated the Standards?
options: Yes. He has violated I(B), because the database is a gift from a broker.
Yes. He has violated VI(C), because this is a referral fee.
No. Soft dollars may pay for research that benefits clients, provided best execution is achieved.
questions.explanation: Using client brokerage for research that benefits those clients, with best execution and disclosure, is consistent with III(A). It isn't a personal gift that compromises him, and it isn't a payment for recommending products or services.

questions.stem: Lisa, CFA, works in a country whose regulations require records to be kept for five years. Her firm deletes records after five years. Has she violated the Standards?
options: No. The seven-year guidance applies only when no regulation sets a period.
Yes. The Code requires seven years, which is stricter than local law.
Yes. Records must be kept indefinitely.
questions.explanation: V(C) requires appropriate records. The seven-year figure is CFA Institute's recommendation for cases where no regulatory requirement exists, not a binding minimum. Here a regulation sets the period. No indefinite retention rule exists.

questions.stem: Ola, CFA, supervises a team. The firm's compliance system is adequate, and staff receive regular training. One of her analysts front-runs client orders despite this. Ola detects it quickly through monitoring, investigates, and restricts the analyst's trading. Has Ola violated IV(C)?
options: Yes. Supervisors are responsible for every violation by their staff.
No. She made reasonable efforts to prevent and detect violations.
Yes. The violation occurred despite her procedures.
questions.explanation: IV(C) requires reasonable efforts, not a guarantee that no violation will ever happen. Adequate procedures, training, monitoring and a prompt response show those efforts were made, so the analyst's breach isn't hers.

flashcards.front: Five-step method for an ethics question
flashcards.back: Who is acting → whose interest → which Standard → requirement met (timing, form, who was told)? → choose the exact remedy.
Recommended or encouraged, NOT required: GIPS compliance, 7-year retention, written allocation policy, firewalls, specific CE hours, reporting violations to regulators or CFA Institute.
Avoid or disclose: VI(A). Disclose: VI(C), V(B). Written consent: IV(B). Notify and get consent: IV(A) independent practice. Decline: I(B), I(E). Dissociate: I(A). Don't act: II(A).
III(B): fairness between clients. VI(B): clients (and employer) before your own account.

flashcards.front: IV(C): when is the supervisor NOT in violation?
flashcards.back: When adequate procedures, training and monitoring were in place and a detected violation was dealt with promptly. The standard is reasonable efforts, not a guarantee.
